(Surat al-Qamar)
Fifty-five verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic."﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ The beginning of the surah is connected to the end of what precedes it, which is His saying: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]. It is as if He repeated that with proof. He said, "I have said: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near,﴾ and it is true, since the moon has split." All the exegetes agree that what is meant is that the moon split and the splitting occurred in it. Reports have indicated the hadith of the splitting, and in the Sahih there is a well-known report narrated by a group of Companions, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked for a specific sign, a miracle, the splitting, so he asked his Lord, and it split, and he went on. Some exegetes said: what is meant is "it will split," but this is far-fetched and has no meaning, because whoever denies it, namely the philosopher, denies it in both the past and the future, while whoever affirms it has no need for interpretation. That view was taken only because the splitting is a tremendous matter; if it had occurred, it would have covered the face of the earth, and so it should have reached the level of tawatur (mass transmission). We say: since the Prophet ﷺ was challenging with the Qur'an, and they used to say, "We produce the most eloquent speech," and they were unable to do so, the Qur'an became a lasting miracle until the Day of Resurrection, so he did not need another miracle, and therefore the scholars did not transmit it to the level of tawatur. As for the historians, they left it out, because histories are mostly used by astrologers, and when the event occurred they said it was like an eclipse of the moon, or the appearance of something in the sky in the shape of half a moon in another place, so they omitted its account from their histories. The Qur'an is the strongest proof and the most powerful affirmation of it, its possibility is beyond doubt, and the Truthful One has reported it, so it is obligatory to believe in its occurrence. The claim that tearing and mending are impossible is the saying of the base, and it has been established that tearing and disruption of the heavens is permissible, and we have mentioned this many times, so we will not repeat it.

And His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic."﴾ Its meaning: after this, if they see a sign, they say, "It is magic," for they have seen earthly signs and heavenly signs and did not believe, and did not abandon their obstinacy; so if they see what they see after this, they will not believe. There is another view: that their habit is that if they see a sign they turn away, and when they saw the splitting of the moon they turned away in accordance with that habit. In this there are several issues:

The first: His saying ﴿sign﴾ — what is it? We say: it is the sign of the drawing near of the Hour, for the splitting of the moon is one of its signs, and they rejected and denied it; so if they see other signs they will also turn away. Or it is the sign of the splitting, for it is a miracle. As for it being a miracle, that is most evident. As for it being a sign of the Hour, that is because the denier of the Lord of the worlds denies the splitting and cleaving of the sky, and likewise his claim about every heavenly body among the stars; so if some of them split, what he says is refuted, and it becomes clear that the ruin of the world is possible. Most exegetes said: its meaning is that among the signs of the establishment of the Hour is the splitting of the moon in the near future, and this is weak. What drove them to this view was the narrowness of the place and the obscurity of the matter to minds. The proof of its weakness is that if God had informed in His Book that the moon will split, and this is a sign of the establishment of the Hour, then that would be a matter that must occur, like the emergence of the beast of the earth and the rising of the sun from the west, and so it would not be a miracle of the Prophet ﷺ, just as these things are wonders and not miracles of the Prophet. It cannot be said: the report of it before its occurrence is a miracle, for we say: then this would be of the kind of reporting the unseen, and so it would not be a miracle in itself, and that is false. Nor can it be said: that was a miracle and a sign, and God informed in the earlier scriptures and books that it would be a miracle of the Prophet ﷺ and that the Hour would be near at that time; this is because the mission of the Prophet ﷺ is a sign already present, as he said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and for this reason it is reported of Satih that when he was informed of the existence of the Prophet ﷺ he spoke of matters that would occur, so his existence was a proof of matters. Also, when the moon split, its splitting occurred at the time the Prophet ﷺ was arguing against the polytheists, who were heedless of what is in the books; as for the People of the Book, they had no need to have the sign of the Hour explained to them, because they affirmed it and its nearness. So it is then a sign indicating the permissibility of the destruction of the heavens, and this is the greatest pillar, for if the heavens are folded up and that is permitted, then the earth and whoever is upon it are not far-fetched to perish. Given this, we say: the meaning of ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ may be in minds and intellects; one says: whoever hears a matter that does not occur considers it distant and far-fetched. This is a good view, although some weak-minded people deny it. This is because interpreting it as near in time rather than in possibility enables the disbeliever to make a corrupt argument: he says, "God said in the Prophet's time: ﴿has drawn near,﴾" and they also say that before that, in the earlier books, He said: ﴿and the promise has drawn near﴾ [al-Anbiya: 97], then a hundred years passed and it did not occur, and it is not unlikely that another thousand years will pass and it will not occur. If the application of the word "near" in time to such a thing were valid, no trust would remain in the reports. Also, His saying ﴿has drawn near﴾ is for seizing the opportunity and faith before faith ceases to be valid, so the disbeliever may say: if nearness is in this sense, then there is no fear of it, for it will not reach me, nor reach my children, nor my children's children. When its possibility is near in the intellects, that is a decisive refutation of the polytheists and philosophers. God, glory be to Him, first required recognition of the Oneness and the Last Day, and said: know that the gathering is certain; the polytheist and the philosopher opposed, and he was not content with merely denying what the Law has explained; he did not say, "it will not occur" or "it is not to be," but said, "that is distant," and was not content with this either, but said, "that is impossible," and was not content with this either, but said, "its impossibility is necessary," for their doctrine is that the restoration of what is non-existent and the revival of the dead is impossible by necessity. For this reason they said: ﴿When we are dead?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82], ﴿When we are bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11], ﴿When we are lost in the earth?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10], using the interrogative in the sense of denial, despite the matter being manifest. So when they considered it distant, God and His Messenger did not suffice with explaining its occurrence, but said: ﴿Indeed the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Hajj: 7], and did not limit himself to this, but said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], and did not leave it until He said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾, ﴿and the true promise has drawn near﴾ [al-Anbiya: 97], ﴿Their reckoning has drawn near for mankind﴾ [al-Anbiya: 1], a rational nearness: it is not permissible to deny what occurs in the twinkling of an eye, for it is easy for God, just as turning the eyeball is easy for us, indeed it is much nearer than that. What strengthens this is the saying of the common people: the time of the world's existence is a long time, and what remains compared with the past is a small thing; therefore He said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near.﴾

As for His saying, peace be upon him: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," its meaning is: there is no prophet after me, for my time extends until the establishment of the Hour, so my time and the Hour are adjacent like these two. There is no doubt that the time is the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and as long as his commands are in force, the time is his, even if he is not in it, just as the place where the king's commands are in force is the king's place, and it is said to be the lands of so-and-so. If it is said: how can it be interpreted as nearness in the rational sense when it is definite? I say: just as His saying, exalted is He, is valid: ﴿Perhaps the Hour will be near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], for "perhaps" expresses hope, while the matter is known to God. Its benefit is that the establishment of the Hour is possible, not in a remote possibility beyond customary limits, like carrying a human being of great weight in our time, or covering a great distance in a short time, which is possible but remote; whereas turning the eyeball is possible in a very near sense.

The second issue: the group whose plural pronoun is the waw in His saying ﴿they see﴾ and ﴿they turn away﴾ is not mentioned, so who are they? We say: they are known, and they are the disbelievers; its meaning is: these disbelievers, if they see a sign, they turn away.

The third issue: the indefiniteness in "sign" is for magnification, i.e., if they see a strong or great sign, they turn away.

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and say, "continuous magic"﴾ — what is the benefit of it? We say: its benefit is to show that the sign is free from any taint of doubt, and that acknowledgment was incumbent upon them because they could not say, "We produce the like of it," and to show that they were turning away without an excuse, for one who turns away as one busy with an important matter, having not looked at the sign, is not blamed for turning away as one is blamed who looks to its end, is unable to attribute it to anyone, and yet claims to bring its like, and then says, "This is nothing, this is magic"; for there is no sign but that the obstinate person can say this about it.

The fifth issue: what is "continuous" (mustamirr)? We say: there are several meanings:

One of them: constant, for Muhammad ﷺ used to bring in every age a miracle, verbal or practical, earthly or heavenly, and they said, "This is ﴿continuous magic﴾," constant and not varying with respect to the Prophet, peace be upon him, unlike the magic of magicians, for some of them are able to do one or two or three things and are unable to do others, whereas he is able to do all.

The second: continuous, i.e., strong, from a strongly twisted rope, from "mirrah," which is strength.

The third: from "bitterness," i.e., bitter magic, abhorrent.

The fourth: continuous, i.e., passing and gone, for magic has no permanence.

He said: ﴿And I have come to you from Sheba with certain news﴾ [al-Naml: 22], because it was a great report. Verification is required only regarding what involves a ruling and results in a matter of significance. Likewise He said: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 44]. Some scholars said that the intended meaning is the Qur'an, and the sense is: the news came in it. It was also said that His words ﴿there had come to them of the news﴾ include everything in the Qur'an of rebukes and admonitions. As for "mā" (that which) in ﴿mā fīhi muzdajar﴾, there are two possibilities:

The first: it is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), meaning: there came to you that which contains a deterrent.

The second: it is a descriptive (mawsūfah), its sense being: "there came to you of the news" a thing described as containing a deterrent. This is more apparent. As for al-muzdajar (the deterrent) in it, there are two possibilities:

The first: izdijār (the act of being deterred).

Then He said, ﴿far-reaching wisdom﴾. There are several interpretations of this:

The first, according to the one who says that in ﴿And there had certainly come to them of the news﴾ what is meant is the Qur'an: ﴿far-reaching wisdom﴾ is in apposition (*badal*), as if He had said: "And there had certainly come to them far-reaching wisdom."

The second: the sending down of that which contains the news is ﴿far-reaching wisdom﴾.

As for His saying ﴿so what do the warnings avail?﴾, there are two interpretations.

One: "what" is a negation particle, and the meaning is that the warners were not sent to compel and force their people to the truth; they were sent only as conveyors of the message. The first: it is in accordance with the view of the one who says, "yakhshaʿna abṣāruhum" (their eyes will be humbled, with the verb feminine), following the manner of the one who says, "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me).

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Hastening to the caller﴾, that is, rushing toward him in submission, ﴿the disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ It is possible that the governing element (al-'amil al-nasib) of "the day" (yawm) in His words ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ is: that is, "the day the caller calls": ﴿the disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ And in this there are two benefits. The first: a reminder to the believer that this day is difficult only for the disbeliever, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So that day will be a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 9, 10], meaning that for him there is hardship with no ease accompanying it. The second: that both matters (the two situations) are common to and shared by the believer and the disbeliever, for the coming out from the graves is as if they were locusts, and the turning toward the caller applies to the believer, for he fears and does not feel safe from punishment except by God's granting him faith, so God gives him reward, and the disbeliever remains, and says: ﴿This is a difficult day.﴾

Then God, exalted is He, repeated some of the reports, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant and said, "He is mad," and he was rebuffed.﴾ In this there is consolation and making light (of the matter) for the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), for his situation is like the situation of those who came before him. And in this there are issues:

First issue: attaching a feminine pronoun to the verb before mentioning the subject is permissible by consensus and good, whereas attaching a plural pronoun to it is considered ugly by most scholars, so they do not allow "kadhdhabu qawma Nuh" (they denied the people of Noah), but they allow "kadhdhabat" (she denied). What is the difference? We say: the feminization before the plural is because femininity and masculinity of the doer is a matter that does not change, and femininity did not come to the doer because of its act which is its doing. So when we say "daraba hadhihi" (this one struck), it does not mean that this one became female because of the striking. Unlike the plural, because plurality of the doers is due to their act which they perform. For when we say "jam' daraba" (a group struck) and "they are strikers" (hum daribun), mere gathering in existence does not validate our saying "daraba" and "hum daribun," because if they gather in one place they are a group, but if not all of them strike, our saying "they struck" is not valid. So the plural pronoun of the verb "fa'iluna" (the doers) gathered them due to their gathering in the act and the doership, not due to the act itself. Therefore it is not permissible to say "daraba jam'" (they struck, a group), because plurality is only understood by the fact that all of them struck. So it is necessary first to know their gathering in the act, and say: "the strikers struck." As for "daraba Hind" (Hind struck), it is correct, because it is not valid to say: femininity was only understood by the fact that she struck; rather she was female, so striking occurred from her and she became a striker. Plurality is not that they were a group and then struck and became strikers; rather they became strikers because of their gathering in the act. Therefore the plural came after the feminine form on the word: "daribah" and "daribat," and the word was not pluralized first for a female or for a male. For this reason it is not good to say "daraba Hind" in the plural sense, while "daraba qawm" and "al-muslimun" (the Muslims struck) are agreed to be good.

Second issue: When God said "kadhdhabat" (she denied), what is the benefit of His words "fa-kadhdhabu 'abdana" (so they denied Our servant)? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

First: His words "kadhdhabat qablahum qawmu Nuh" mean "with Our signs and the sign of the splitting (of the moon), so they denied."

Second: "kadhdhabat qawmu Nuhin al-mursalin" [ash-Shu'ara: 105], and they said: God did not send any messenger, and they denied them regarding tawhid. "Fa-kadhdhabu 'abdana" (so they denied Our servant) as they denied others. That is because the people of Noah were polytheists who worshipped idols, and whoever worships idols denies every messenger and rejects prophethood, because he says: God has no connection with the lower world; His command is with the stars. So their doctrine was denial, and so they denied.

Third: His words "fa-kadhdhabu 'abdana" are for confirmation and a response against them; the sense is: "kadhdhabat qawmu Nuh," and their denial of Our servant was not a denial in truth, as a speaker says: "he denied me," then he denied a truthful person.

Third issue: Very often God specifically singles out the righteous by attributing them to Himself, as in His words ﴿Indeed My servants﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], ﴿O My servants﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68], ﴿Remember Our servant﴾ [Sad: 41], ﴿Indeed he is of Our servants﴾ [as-Saffat: 132], while each one is His servant. What is the secret in this? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects.

First: what is said in the well-known view, that attributing them to Himself is an honour from Him; whoever is singled out by being His servant is honoured. This is like His words ﴿that purify My House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125] and His words ﴿the she-camel of God﴾ [ash-Shams: 13].

Second: what is meant by "Our servant" is: the one who worshipped Us. All are servants, for they were created for worship, according to His words ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 56]. But among them is one who worshipped and thereby realized the purpose, so he became His servant. This is supported by His words ﴿Be servants to Me﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 79], meaning: realize the purpose.

Third: attribution conveys exclusivity, so the meaning of "Our servant" is the one who does not take any worshipped other than Us, and whoever follows his desire has taken a god. The servant who is attributed is the one who, wholly and at every time, belongs to God; his eating, drinking and all his affairs are for the sake of God, Exalted, "and few are they" (wa-qalilun ma hum).

Fourth issue: What is the benefit in choosing the word "servant" ('abd), when if he had said "Our messenger" (rasuluna) it would have shown more clearly the ugliness of their act? We say: His words "'abdana" are more indicative of his truthfulness and the ugliness of their denial than "rasulana" would be, because a servant distorts the speech of his master less than a messenger does, so it is like His words ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46].

Fifth issue: His words "wa-qalu majnun" (and they said: mad) point to the fact that he brought signs indicating his truthfulness, since they saw what they were unable to match, and they said: he is afflicted by jinn. Or it is to add explanation of the ugliness of their conduct, since they were not content with saying he is a liar, but said: mad, meaning he says what no sane person would accept, whereas a lying sane person says what he thinks will appear truthful. So they said "majnun," meaning he says what no sane person has said, thereby showing their exaggeration in denial.

Sixth issue: "wa-zdujir" (and he was rebuffed) is either a report from God, exalted is He, or a quotation of their words. Scholars differ on this. Some said: it is a report from God, exalted is He, and it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "kadhdhabu" and "qalu," meaning: they denied, and he was rebuffed, that is, harmed and driven off, like His words ﴿they were denied and harmed﴾ [al-An'am: 34]. On this view, if it is said: had He said "kadhdhabu 'abdana wa-zajarahu" (they denied Our servant and drove him off), the speech would have been more fitting. We say: no, rather this is more eloquent, because the aim is to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning those who came before him. He said "wa-zdujir," meaning they did what requires being driven off, namely their calling (him), until he left off calling them and turned from calling to faith to calling against them. Had He said "zajarahu" (they drove him off), it would not convey that he was harmed by them; for in the ordinary usage one says "they harmed me" (adhawni) but "I was not harmed" (ma ta'adhdhaytu); whereas "ू'dhītu" (I was harmed) is like the intransitive, said only when the act has occurred, not before it. Others said: "wa-zdujir" is a quotation of their words, meaning: they said "zdujir," the sense being they said "majnun mzdujar" (mad, driven off), and its meaning: the jinn drove him off, or as if they said: "he has gone mad and been driven off." The first view is more correct, and what follows from it is established.

Second: "kadhdhabat qawmu Nuhin al-mursalin" [ash-Shu'ara: 105], and they said: God did not send any messenger, and they denied them regarding tawhid. "Fa-kadhdhabu 'abdana" (so they denied Our servant) as they denied others. That is because the people of Noah were polytheists who worshipped idols, and whoever worships idols denies every messenger and rejects prophethood, because he says: God has no connection with the lower world; His command is with the stars. So their doctrine was denial, and so they denied.

Third: His words "fa-kadhdhabu 'abdana" are for confirmation and a response against them; the sense is: "kadhdhabat qawmu Nuh," and their denial of Our servant was not a denial in truth, as a speaker says: "he denied me," then he denied a truthful person.

Third issue: Very often God specifically singles out the righteous by attributing them to Himself, as in His words ﴿Indeed My servants﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], ﴿O My servants﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68], ﴿Remember Our servant﴾ [Sad: 41], ﴿Indeed he is of Our servants﴾ [as-Saffat: 132], while each one is His servant. What is the secret in this? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects.

First: what is said in the well-known view, that attributing them to Himself is an honour from Him; whoever is singled out by being His servant is honoured. This is like His words ﴿that purify My House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125] and His words ﴿the she-camel of God﴾ [ash-Shams: 13].

Second: what is meant by "Our servant" is: the one who worshipped Us. All are servants, for they were created for worship, according to His words ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 56]. But among them is one who worshipped and thereby realized the purpose, so he became His servant. This is supported by His words ﴿Be servants to Me﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 79], meaning: realize the purpose.

Third: attribution conveys exclusivity, so the meaning of "Our servant" is the one who does not take any worshipped other than Us, and whoever follows his desire has taken a god. The servant who is attributed is the one who, wholly and at every time, belongs to God; his eating, drinking and all his affairs are for the sake of God, Exalted, "and few are they" (wa-qalilun ma hum).

Fourth issue: What is the benefit in choosing the word "servant" ('abd), when if he had said "Our messenger" (rasuluna) it would have shown more clearly the ugliness of their act? We say: His words "'abdana" are more indicative of his truthfulness and the ugliness of their denial than "rasulana" would be, because a servant distorts the speech of his master less than a messenger does, so it is like His words ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–46].

Fifth issue: His words "wa-qalu majnun" (and they said: mad) point to the fact that he brought signs indicating his truthfulness, since they saw what they were unable to match, and they said: he is afflicted by jinn. Or it is to add explanation of the ugliness of their conduct, since they were not content with saying he is a liar, but said: mad, meaning he says what no sane person would accept, whereas a lying sane person says what he thinks will appear truthful. So they said "majnun," meaning he says what no sane person has said, thereby showing their exaggeration in denial.

Sixth issue: "wa-zdujir" (and he was rebuffed) is either a report from God, exalted is He, or a quotation of their words. Scholars differ on this. Some said: it is a report from God, exalted is He, and it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "kadhdhabu" and "qalu," meaning: they denied, and he was rebuffed, that is, harmed and driven off, like His words ﴿they were denied and harmed﴾ [al-An'am: 34]. On this view, if it is said: had He said "kadhdhabu 'abdana wa-zajarahu" (they denied Our servant and drove him off), the speech would have been more fitting. We say: no, rather this is more eloquent, because the aim is to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning those who came before him. He said "wa-zdujir," meaning they did what requires being driven off, namely their calling (him), until he left off calling them and turned from calling to faith to calling against them. Had He said "zajarahu" (they drove him off), it would not convey that he was harmed by them; for in the ordinary usage one says "they harmed me" (adhawni) but "I was not harmed" (ma ta'adhdhaytu); whereas "ू'dhītu" (I was harmed) is like the intransitive, said only when the act has occurred, not before it. Others said: "wa-zdujir" is a quotation of their words, meaning: they said "zdujir," the sense being they said "majnun mzdujar" (mad, driven off), and its meaning: the jinn drove him off, or as if they said: "he has gone mad and been driven off." The first view is more correct, and what follows from it is established.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Hastening to the caller﴾, that is, rushing toward him in submission, ﴿the disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ It is possible that the governing element (al-'amil al-nasib) of "the day" (yawm) in His words ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ is: that is, "the day the caller calls": ﴿the disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ And in this there are two benefits. The first: a reminder to the believer that this day is difficult only for the disbeliever, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So that day will be a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 9, 10], meaning that for him there is hardship with no ease accompanying it. The second: that both matters (the two situations) are common to and shared by the believer and the disbeliever, for the coming out from the graves is as if they were locusts, and the turning toward the caller applies to the believer, for he fears and does not feel safe from punishment except by God's granting him faith, so God gives him reward, and the disbeliever remains, and says: ﴿This is a difficult day.﴾

Then God, exalted is He, repeated some of the reports, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant and said, "He is mad," and he was rebuffed.﴾ In this there is consolation and making light (of the matter) for the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), for his situation is like the situation of those who came before him. And in this there are issues:

First issue: attaching a feminine pronoun to the verb before mentioning the subject is permissible by consensus and good, whereas attaching a plural pronoun to it is considered ugly by most scholars, so they do not allow "kadhdhabu qawma Nuh" (they denied the people of Noah), but they allow "kadhdhabat" (she denied). What is the difference? We say: the feminization before the plural is because femininity and masculinity of the doer is a matter that does not change, and femininity did not come to the doer because of its act which is its doing. So when we say "daraba hadhihi" (this one struck), it does not mean that this one became female because of the striking. Unlike the plural, because plurality of the doers is due to their act which they perform. For when we say "jam' daraba" (a group struck) and "they are strikers" (hum daribun), mere gathering in existence does not validate our saying "daraba" and "hum daribun," because if they gather in one place they are a group, but if not all of them strike, our saying "they struck" is not valid. So the plural pronoun of the verb "fa'iluna" (the doers) gathered them due to their gathering in the act and the doership, not due to the act itself. Therefore it is not permissible to say "daraba jam'" (they struck, a group), because plurality is only understood by the fact that all of them struck. So it is necessary first to know their gathering in the act, and say: "the strikers struck." As for "daraba Hind" (Hind struck), it is correct, because it is not valid to say: femininity was only understood by the fact that she struck; rather she was female, so striking occurred from her and she became a striker. Plurality is not that they were a group and then struck and became strikers; rather they became strikers because of their gathering in the act. Therefore the plural came after the feminine form on the word: "daribah" and "daribat," and the word was not pluralized first for a female or for a male. For this reason it is not good to say "daraba Hind" in the plural sense, while "daraba qawm" and "al-muslimun" (the Muslims struck) are agreed to be good.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ is an arrangement of the utmost beauty, because when they rebuked him and he withdrew from calling them, he called upon his Lord, "I am overcome." Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: "Inni" (إنِّي) has been read with a kasra on the hamza, as a direct supplication, so it is as if he said, "I am overcome." It has also been read with a fatha, meaning "because I am overcome" (bi-anni).

The second issue: What is the meaning of "maghlub" (مَغْلُوبٌ, overcome)? We say: there are several interpretations.

The first: "The unbelievers have overcome me, so help me against them."

The second: "My own self (nafs) has overcome me and driven me to invoke [destruction] upon them, so help me against my self." This interpretation was transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyya, and it is weak.

The third: a view combining the two, which is better than them both, and it is that one says: the Prophet (ﷺ) does not invoke [destruction] upon his people as long as there remains in his soul forbearance and patience, and his patience continues for as long as faith among them is still hoped for. Then, when their harm had come and the hope of patience vanished after a period of time, this is evidenced by the saying of God Exalted to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief [over them]﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 3], ﴿So let not your soul expire in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8]. And God Exalted said: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed they are to be drowned﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 27]. Then Noah said: "O my Lord, indeed my soul has overcome me, and it has commanded me to invoke [destruction] upon them, so destroy them." So its meaning is: "I am overcome" by the judgment of human nature, that is, I have been overpowered and my patience has been exhausted, so help me against them, not against my self.

The third issue: "Fa-intasir" (فَانْتَصِرْ) means "help me" or "avenge yourself" [on them], for they disbelieved in you. Concerning this there are several interpretations:

One of them: "So help me" corresponds to his saying "overcome."

The second: "So help yourself and your religion, for I have been overcome and have been unable to defend your religion."

The third: "So defend the truth," and no mention of himself or of his Lord is made in it. This is what a person of strong soul says when the truth is with him: one says, "O God, destroy the liar among us, and support the one who is in the right among us."

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring forth﴾, immediately after his supplication. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Are "opening" (fath), "gates" (abwab) and "heaven" (sama') to be taken in their literal senses, or is it figurative? We say: there are two views concerning this. One of them: they are literal, and heaven has gates that are opened and closed, and there is no improbability in this. The second: it is by way of metaphor (isti'arah, a figure of speech in which a word is used for something other than its literal meaning). The apparent sense is that the water came from the clouds, and on this view it is like when one says of heavy rain, "The spouts of heaven flowed and the mouths of the water-skins were opened," meaning as if that were so. The rain in the Flood was such that one would say, "The gates of heaven were opened," and there is no doubt that the rain from above was in the utmost abundance.

The second issue: God's saying ﴿So We opened﴾ is a statement that God took vengeance upon them and punished them with water, not with an army He sent down, as He said: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from heaven, nor were We ever to send [one]﴾ [Ya-Sin: 28], ﴿It was but one shriek﴾ [Ya-Sin: 29], as a demonstration of perfect power. And it is remarkable that they had been asking for rain for years, so He destroyed them with what they had sought.

The third issue: What is the function of the "ba'" (ب) in His saying ﴿with water pouring forth﴾, and how is it positioned? We say: there are two views:

One of them: it is as in the saying of one who says, "I opened the door with the key." Its sense is that one imagines as if the water came and opened the gate. On this is based the explanation of the statement of one who says, "May God open for you with goodness," meaning He decrees a good that comes and opens the door. On this view there is a subtle point, one of the marvels of meanings: the intended object is presented as preceding in existence, as if one's goal came to a closed door, opened it and reached you. Likewise the saying of one who says, "Perhaps God will open with provision," meaning He decrees a provision that comes to the door which is like a locked one, pushes it and opens it, so God has opened it by means of provision.

The second: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven﴾ is joined with ﴿water pouring forth﴾. Al-infihar (الِانْهِمارُ) is the pouring out and the downpour with intense force. The verification of this is that the rain issues from the heaven, which is the cloud, as one issuing forth dripping from its container. On that day it was issuing forth like something released and pouring out from a gate.

[p. 34]

Then God Most High said: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ ﴿so the waters met for a matter already decreed﴾. In it there is eloquence that is not found in the saying of one who says: "And We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth." This is an instance of tamyiz (specification) in many places: when you say "Zayd's breast was constricted (dhar'an)," you affirm what your saying "the breast of Zayd was constricted" does not affirm. In it there are several issues:

The first issue: He said ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ and did not say "And We opened the heaven with gates," because the heaven is greater than the earth, and [the verse] is for hyperbole (mubalagha). For this reason He said ﴿the gates of heaven﴾, and He did not say "pipes," nor "openings," nor "channels," nor other than these.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾, it is more eloquent than the saying "And We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth," because it is literal and there is no hyperbole in it. For the correctness of that statement it suffices that He place in the earth three springs. With this, and in the heaven, nothing suits except the saying of one who says: "Then We sent down from the sky water, or waters." Something like what we have mentioned is in meaning, not in miraculousness. The wisdom is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth?﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], where there is no hyperbole. His speech is not comparable to the speech of God, nor does it come close to it; but I have mentioned it as an example: ﴿And to God belongs the highest example﴾ [al-Nahl: 60].

The second issue: Is "uyun" (springs) in "uyun al-ma'" (springs of water) literal or figurative? We say: the well-known view is that the word ʿayn (ʿayn, "eye/spring") is homonymous (mushtarak), and the apparent view is that it is literal for the ʿayn which is the instrument of sight, and figurative for other things. As for "springs of water," it is because they resemble the seeing eye from which tears flow, or because the water in the spring is like the light in the eye. However, it is a well-known figurative usage that has become so dominant that it does not require a qarina (contextual indicator) in use, except to distinguish between the two meanings of ʿayn. Just as the word is not taken to mean the seeing eye without a qarina, so it is not taken to mean the gushing spring without a qarina, such as: "I drank from the ʿayn and bathed in it," and other matters found in a spring (yanbu'). It is said: ʿanahu yaʿinuhu (ʿanahu, "he afflicted him with the evil eye") when he struck him with the evil eye; and ʿayyanahu taʿyinan ("he specified/designated it"), its literal sense being: he made it such that the eye falls upon it; and ʿaynahu muʿayanatan wa ʿiyanan ("he saw it with his own eyes"); and ʿayyana: became such that the eye falls upon it.

The third issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so the waters met﴾ was recited as "fa-iltaqa al-mā'ān" (the two waters met), i.e., the two kinds of it: the water of the sky and the water of the earth. Names of kinds (asma' al-ajnas) are made dual according to the interpretation of "a type," and they are also made plural: it is said "ʿindī tamrān" (I have two dates), "tumūr" and "atmār" according to the interpretation of "two kinds" and "kinds" of it. The sound and well-known reading is ﴿so the waters met﴾, and it has a subtle meaning: when He, Exalted is He, said ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with pouring water﴾, He mentioned the water and mentioned the inhimar (pouring), which is descent with force. Then when He said ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾, it was of beautiful eloquence to say something that indicates that the water gushed out of it with force, so He said ﴿so the waters met﴾, meaning: the water boiled forth from the spring with force until it rose up and met the water of the sky. Had it flowed with a weak flow, it would not have met the water of the sky; rather the water of the sky would have come upon it and joined with it. Perhaps what is meant by His saying ﴿and the oven boiled over﴾ [Hud: 40] is something like this.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for a matter already decreed﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: for a state which God Most High had determined as He willed.

The second: for a state in which He measured one of the two waters by the measure of the other.

The third: for all measures, because people differed: some said the water of the sky was greater, some said the water of the earth, and some said they were equal. So He said: "for whatever measure it was." The first indicates the greatness of the matter of the Flood, for the indefiniteness of "amr" (matter) conveys that. A speaker says: "Something befell so-and-so that cannot be described," indicating its magnitude. There is another possibility: that it is said "the waters met," meaning they gathered for the matter of their destruction, which was predestined and decreed. In this there is a refutation of the astrologers who say that the Flood was caused by the conjunction of the seven planets around a watery zodiac sign, and that drowning was not intended in itself; rather it was a consequence necessarily entailed by the Flood's occurrence. So He said: that did not happen except for a matter already decreed. This is indicated by God Most High's revelation to Noah that they were among the drowned.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We carried him upon [a vessel] made of planks and nails﴾ ﴿running under Our eyes﴾. That is, a ship. He omitted the noun modified and put the adjective in its place, as an indication that it was made of planks fitted together and fastened with nails (dusur), and that its coming apart would be extremely easy, yet it did not happen, and that is by the grace of Allah. Dusur means nails.

As for His saying ﴿running﴾, that is, a ship of planks, running. As for His saying ﴿under Our eyes﴾, that is, in Our sight, or under Our protection; because the eye is the instrument of that, so it is used for it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verse 14:

And His saying, Most High: ﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved﴾ admits of several aspects:

The first: its accusative case (nasb) is governed by His saying ﴿and We carried him﴾, meaning: We carried him as a recompense, that is, so that that carrying would be a recompense for his patience in the face of their disbelief (kufran).

The second: it is governed by His saying ﴿sailing under Our eyes﴾, because it carries the sense of "Our protecting," meaning: We did not leave him, away from Our eyes and Our help, as a recompense for him.

The third: it is governed by an act that results from the whole of what was mentioned, as if He had said: "We opened the gates of heaven, caused the earth to burst forth with springs, and carried him," and all of that We did as a recompense for him. We mention this because the recompense would not have been realized except by His preserving him and saving him from them, so it is necessary that "recompense" be in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) governed by these acts. Let us mention the subtleties it contains in several issues:

The first issue: He said, regarding the sky: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven﴾, because the sky possesses return (raj') and has no fissures (futur); and He did not say "We split the sky." And He said, regarding the earth: ﴿and We caused the earth to burst forth﴾, because it possesses cleavage (sad').

The second: since rain was made like water issuing from wide open gates, and He did not say of the earth "and We made to flow from the earth seas and rivers," but rather said ﴿springs (uyun)﴾, and what issues from a spring is less than what issues from a gate, He mentioned regarding the earth that He caused all of it to burst forth, saying ﴿and We caused the earth to burst forth﴾, so that the abundance of the earth's springs would correspond to the vastness of the gates of heaven, and thus what was achieved here by abundance is achieved there by vastness.

The third: at the time of wrath He mentioned the cause of destruction, namely the opening of the gates of heaven and the bursting of the earth with springs, and He alluded to the destruction by His saying ﴿upon a matter that had been decreed﴾, that is, the matter of destruction, without stating it explicitly. At the time of mercy He mentioned the revelation explicitly by His saying ﴿and We carried him﴾, and He alluded to the path of salvation by His saying ﴿possessed of planks and nails﴾. Likewise He said elsewhere: ﴿So the flood seized them﴾ and did not say "so they were destroyed," and He said: ﴿So We saved him and the people of the ship﴾, explicitly stating the saving and not explicitly stating the destruction, as an indication of the vastness of mercy and the utmost of generosity. That is: We created the cause of destruction, but had they returned, that cause would not have harmed them, as He, ﷺ, said: ﴿O my son, ride with us﴾ [Hud: 42]. And at the time of saving, He saved him and made a path to salvation, which is the taking of the ship; and even had it broken, it would not have harmed him, but would have saved him. So the aim at the time of saving is salvation, hence He mentioned the place (mahall), and the aim at the time of destruction is the manifestation of might, hence He mentioned the cause explicitly.

The fourth: His saying, Most High: ﴿sailing under Our eyes﴾ is more eloquent than "Our protecting." One says, "Make this the object of your eye (nusb aynika)," and does not say "guard it," seeking intensification.

The fifth: ﴿under Our eyes﴾ may admit that what is meant is Our protecting; for this reason it is said: "Sight is the tongue of the eye."

The sixth: He said: that was a recompense for what they disbelieved in, not for his faith and gratitude; so what was requited was the recompense for his patience in the face of their disbelief, while the recompense for his gratitude to Us remains. It was also read as ﴿jizā'an﴾ with a kasra on the jim, meaning mujāzāh (requital), like qitāl and muqātalah. And it was read ﴿liman kāna kafara﴾ with a fatha on the kaf. As for ﴿kufira﴾, there are two aspects:

One of them: that kufira is like shukira, which takes a preposition and takes none; one says shakartuhu and shakartu lahu. The Most High said: ﴿And be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152], and the Most High said: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256].

The second: that it is from kufr (disbelief) and not from kufran (ingratitude), meaning: a recompense for one whose matter was concealed and whose affair was denied. It may be said that it was "kufira bihi" and the preposition was omitted because the meaning is clear.

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And We have left it as a sign﴾, and regarding what the pronoun in "it" refers back to there are two possibilities.

One of them: it refers to something already mentioned, namely the ship that had planks (al-Safinah allati fiha alwah). On this view there are also two possibilities.

The first: God left its trace (ayn) for a period until it was seen and known, and it was on al-Judi in the Jazirah (the Upper Mesopotamian region), and it was said that it was in the land of India.

The second: its like was left among people, to be mentioned. The second of the first two possibilities is that it refers to something known, i.e., "We left the ship as a sign." The first is more apparent. On this possibility it may be said that ﴿We left it﴾ means "We made it" (ja'alnaha ayah), because after finishing with it, it became left behind and made; a speaker says "I left so-and-so as a mutilated example (mathulah)," meaning "I made him," since we have explained that whoever finishes a matter leaves it and makes it, so he mentions one of the two verbs in place of the other.

As for God's words, exalted: ﴿So is there any who will remember?﴾, this is an indication that the matter from the side of the messengers had been completed, and nothing remained but the side of those to whom they were sent, that they be warned, reflecting, guided by the grace of God. ﴿So is there any who will remember?﴾ meaning: any who is guided. This statement is suitable as an exhortation and suitable as a warning and deterrence. In it there are several issues:

The first: Here He said ﴿And We have left it﴾, and in al-Ankabut He said: ﴿And We made it a sign﴾ [al-Ankabut: 15]. We say: although these two are one in meaning, as explained earlier, the word "leaving" (tark) indicates making and completion over days. So it is as if it is mentioned here in detail, since He explained the rain from the sky and the bursting forth of the earth, and mentioned the ship with His words ﴿possessed of planks and nails﴾, and mentioned its running, so He said ﴿We have left it﴾, indicating the completion of the decreed act. And there He said ﴿We made it﴾, indicating a part of that. If it is said: if the matter is so, how did He say here ﴿And We carried him﴾ without saying "and his companions," while there He said ﴿So We delivered him and the companions of the ship﴾ [al-Ankabut: 15]? We say: the deliverance is mentioned here in a more eloquent way than what He mentioned there, because He said ﴿running under Our eyes﴾, i.e., Our protection, and the protection of the ship is protection of its companions, and protection of their property, their animals, and the living creatures with them. So His words ﴿So We delivered him and the companions of the ship﴾ do not necessarily entail the deliverance of the property except with another explanation. The narration in Surah Hud is more detailed and complete, so He said: ﴿We said: carry in it of every kind two pairs﴾ [Hud: 40], meaning what is carried. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And it settled on al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44], clearly stating the safety of the ship and indicating the safety of everyone in it. As for His words ﴿ayah﴾, it is in the accusative as a second object of "tarak" (left), since it has the meaning of "ja'al" (made), as explained earlier, and this is the apparent reading. It may also be said that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), since you say "I left it while it is a sign" (wa hiya ayah). Although it is not in the pattern of the active or passive participle, it has that meaning, as if He said: "We left it indicating." It may also be said that its accusative is a specifier (tamyiz), since it is one aspect of the leaving, like the saying "I struck him with a whip."

The second issue: ﴿muddakir﴾ is a form of (mufta'il) from dhakara yadhkuru, and its origin is mudhtakir. Since the articulation point of the dhal is close to that of the ta', and letters of close articulation are difficult to pronounce in succession, when you look at the dhal together with the ta' in pronunciation, the dhal comes close to becoming a ta' and the ta' comes close to becoming a dal. So the ta' was made a dal, then the dal was assimilated into it. Some read according to the original, mudhtakir; some changed the ta' to dal and read muddakir; and some of the philologists say mudhdakir, changing the ta' and not assimilating. Each has its own justification. Al-muddakir is the one who takes heed, the one who reflects. As for His words ﴿muddakir﴾, it is either an indication of what is in His words ﴿Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes'﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], meaning: is there anyone who remembers that state; or an indication of the clarity of the matter, as if the signs of God were obtained by all and they forgot them: ﴿So is there any who will remember﴾ anything of them.

Then God Most High said: ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ On this there are two views.

The first: that this is a question addressed by the Prophet (ﷺ), serving as a reminder to him and a promise of the final outcome.

The second: that it is general, a reminder to all creation, and "nudhur" (warnings) has had the possessive yā' (the ya' of first-person possession) dropped from it, just as the yā' of "yasr" was dropped in the words of God Most High: ﴿And by the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4]. This is done at pause (waqf), and similar examples are numerous, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿So fear Me, and worship Me﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 56], ﴿nor will they be rescued﴾ [Ya-Sin: 43], [al-Zumar: 16], and His words: ﴿O My servants, fear Me﴾ [al-Zumar: 16], and His words: ﴿and do not deny Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. It has also been recited with the yā' affirmed: "'adhabi wa nudhuri" (My punishment and My warnings). On this there are several issues:
