The first: What requires the fā' (the "then") in God Most High's words: ﴿So how was﴾? We say: If we hold that the question is from the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is as if God Most High said to him: "You have known the reports of those who came before you, so how was [their end]," meaning: after knowledge of them has reached you by their transmission. If we hold that the question is general, we say: when He said: ﴿Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15], He supposed their existence and said: O one who remembers, and the state was known through the reminder: ﴿So how was My punishment﴾. It may also be said that it is connected to His words: ﴿Is there anyone who will remember?﴾, its implied sense being "how was My punishment."

The second issue: They did not see the punishment or the warnings, so how is a question put to them? We say: If we hold that the question is from the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is known as far as it is known. If we hold that it is general, then it is on the assumption of remembrance, and on the assumption of remembrance the state is known. It may also be said that it is not a question at all, but an announcement of the greatness of the matter, as in God Most High's words: ﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1, 2] and ﴿The Striking Calamity, what is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 1, 2]. This is because interrogation is sometimes used for announcement, just as the form "hal" is used for interrogation; one says "Zayd is in the house?" meaning "Is Zayd in the house?", and one who fulfils his promise says "Did I keep my word?" It is as if God Most High said: "My punishment has occurred, and how it was," meaning it was great, and then there is no need to know the one being questioned.

The third issue: God Most High had said earlier: ﴿So We opened﴾ [al-Qamar: 11], ﴿and We caused to gush forth﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], and ﴿by Our eyes﴾ [al-Qamar: 14], and He did not say "how was Our punishment." We say, for two reasons.

The first is verbal: the yā' of the speaker may be omitted, since in speech it often falls away when two unvowelled letters meet, as you say "ghulami alladhi" (my boy who) and "dari allati" (my house which). Here it was omitted to harmonise with the endings of the verses. The nūn and the alif in the pronoun of the plural, however, are not omitted.

The second is semantic: if the question is from the Prophet (ﷺ), then the singular pronoun is for "the reports," while in "fatahna" and "fajjarna" it is for frightening the disobedient. We have said that His words "mudhkir" contain an allusion to His words: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; so when the pronoun was made singular by His words ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾, He said "how was."

The fourth issue: "nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir," so is it a verbal noun like "nasib" and "nahib," or an agent noun like "kabir" and "saghir"? We say: most of the exegetes hold that here it is a verbal noun, meaning: how was the outcome of My punishment and the outcome of My warning? The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the reports, that is: how was the outcome of God's enemies and His messengers? Did the punishment befall those who denied the messengers or not? So if you know the state, O Muhammad, then be patient, for the outcome of your affair is like the outcome of those warners. The punishment was not put in the plural because it is a verbal noun; had it been pluralised, there would have been in its plural an assumption and supposition, and there is no need for that. If it is said: God Most High's words ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 23] mean "the warnings" in the sense of the warnings that came to them, while as for messengers, only one came to them, we say: every nation that came before, those who associated partners with God, denied the messengers, and said: "God has sent down nothing," and the polytheists denied them all except Abraham, peace be upon him, whom they regarded as good because he was the elder of the messengers. So it is not said ﴿Thamud denied the warnings﴾ to mean the prophets entirely, just as you polytheists deny them.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ Regarding this there are several aspects:

The first: [It is easy] for memorization, so it can be memorized and is easy to do so. None of God's books other than the Qur'an has been preserved by heart. His saying, ﴿so is there any who will remember?﴾ means: is there anyone who will memorize it and recite it?

The second: We made it easy for admonition, since We have brought in it every kind of wisdom.

The third: We made it such that it clings to hearts and its hearing is delightful. Whoever does not understand it seeks to understand it, and he does not tire of hearing it or of comprehending it, nor does he say, "I already know it, so I will not listen to it." Rather, every hour his delight and knowledge in it increase.

The fourth, and it is the most apparent: when the Prophet (ﷺ) was reminded of the state of Noah (peace be upon him), and Noah had a miracle, it was said to him: Indeed your miracle is the Qur'an. ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ as a reminder for everyone, and you challenge the world with it, and it remains through the passage of ages. Everyone who is present with you does not need supplication and request for the manifestation of a miracle, and after you no one denies the occurrence of what occurred, as some deny the splitting of the moon. His saying, ﴿so is there any who will remember?﴾ means: [is there any] one who remembers (mutadhakkir), because the ifti'al and tafa''ul forms often come with the same meaning. On this basis, if someone says: this requires the existence of a prior matter that was forgotten, we say: what is in the fitrah (innate disposition) of submission to the truth is like the forgotten, so "is there any who will remember" refers to returning to what one was created upon. It has also been said: "is there any who will remember" means: any who will memorize or be admonished, in line with what we explained concerning His saying, ﴿We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ and His saying ﴿so is there any who will remember﴾. According to our view, the intended meaning is "mutadhakkir," indicating the manifestness of the matter, so that it does not need reminding, but is something already present with him, not requiring repetition of what is with others.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verse 18:

Then God Most High said: ﴿ʿĀd denied, so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ Concerning it there are several issues:

First: He said regarding the people of Noah, ﴿The people of Noah denied﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105], and He did not say regarding ʿĀd, "The people of Hud denied." This is because definiteness, whenever it can be expressed in a more eloquent form, is preferable to be expressed in that form, and definiteness by a proper name is preferable to definiteness by an annexation to it. For when you say "the House of God" (bayt Allah), it does not convey what your saying "the Kaʿba" conveys. Likewise, when you say "the Messenger of God" it does not convey what your saying "Muhammad" conveys. So "ʿĀd" is a proper name for the people, and it is not said that "the people of Hud" is more definite, for two reasons:

The first: God Most High described ʿĀd as "the people of Hud" when He said: ﴿Ah, remoteness for ʿĀd, the people of Hud﴾ [Hud: 60]. The more apparent is not described by the less apparent, nor the more specific by the more general.

The second: The people of Hud are one people, and ʿĀd. It has been said that it is a term applied to several peoples, and for this reason God Most High said: ﴿ʿĀd of old﴾ [al-Najm: 50]. We say: As for His saying, ﴿for ʿĀd, the people of Hud﴾, this is not a qualifier (sifa) but an apposition (badal). In an apposition it is permissible for the substitute to be less definite than the thing substituted, and it is permissible to substitute a definite noun with an indefinite one. As for "ʿĀd of old," we have already mentioned that this is to clarify their precedence, i.e., ʿĀd who came before, and it is not for distinguishing and defining them, just as you say "Muhammad the Prophet, my intercessor," "God the Generous, my Lord," and "the Lord of the Honoured Kaʿba," to show nobility and not to identify and define them. Just as you say: "I entered the inhabited house out of the two houses," and "I served the ascetic man out of the two men." Thus the intended purpose of the description becomes clear.

The second issue: He did not say "they denied Hud," as He said: ﴿So they denied Our servant﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]. This is for two reasons.

The first: The denial of Noah was more eloquent and more severe, since he called them for nearly a thousand years and they persisted in denial. For this reason God Most High mentioned the denial of Noah in several places and did not explicitly mention the denial of anyone other than Noah, although He alluded to it in one of them. In al-Aʿraf He said: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾ [Yunus: 73]. He also said, relating from Noah: ﴿He said: My Lord, my people have denied me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 117], and He said: ﴿They have disobeyed me﴾ [Nuh: 21]. In these places He did not explicitly mention the denial of any people other than his own, except rarely. For this reason, in the passages mentioning Shuʿayb, God Most High said "they denied him," and He said ﴿Those who denied Shuʿayb﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 92], and He said, of his people: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 66], because he called his people for a long time.

The second: The narration of ʿĀd is mentioned here in brief, so He mentioned only their denial and their punishment, and said ﴿ʿĀd denied﴾, just as He said ﴿The people of Noah denied﴾, and He did not mention his supplication against them and its answer, as He did regarding Noah.

The third issue: God Most High said ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ before He explained the punishment. In the account of Noah He explained the punishment and then said ﴿how was﴾. What is the wisdom in this? We say: The interrogative that He mentioned in the account of Noah is mentioned here, namely His saying ﴿so how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾, just as He said before and after in the account of Thamud. Except that in the account of ʿĀd, God related "so how was" twice. The first time the interrogative is used to clarify, as a teacher says to one who does not know how a certain matter is: "How is it?" so that the questioned becomes a questioner, and he says, "It is such and such." Likewise here He said ﴿ʿĀd denied, so how was My punishment﴾, and the listener said: "Explain it, for I do not know." So He said: (Indeed We sent...). As for the second time, the interrogative is used to magnify, as the speaker says to one who has witnessed something: "How did you do it and make it?" and he replies, "Excellent what you did," and he says, "You have brought something wondrous," thus affirming the greatness of the deed by the interrogative. He mentioned the first time here and did not mention it in another place because the account was mentioned here in brief, and it would have forfeited the lesson due to the brevity. So He said ﴿so how was My punishment﴾ to urge reflection and contemplation. As for the brevity in their narration, it is because most of their affair was arrogance, reliance on strength, and not paying attention to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is indicated by His saying: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right, and they said: Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. He mentioned their arrogance many times. The people of Muhammad (ﷺ) were not extreme in arrogance; their extremity was in denial and in attributing madness to him. He mentioned the condition of Noah in detail, for his people combined denial with arrogance. Likewise the condition of Salih (peace be upon him) He mentioned in detail, because of its strong resemblance to the condition of Muhammad (ﷺ).

[Page 40]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind, roaring, on a day of continuous misfortune.﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So how was My punishment﴾ with the pronoun in the singular there, and He did not say "Our punishment." Here He said "Indeed We" and did not say "Indeed I." The answer is what we mentioned concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven﴾ [al-Qamar: 11].

The second issue: As for ṣarṣar (violent, roaring) in it, there are several aspects:

The first of them: a wind that is very loud in sound, from ṣarīr (creaking, a shrill sound), and ṣarrah is the intensity of shouting.

The second of them: one that blows continuously, from aṣarra ʿalā al-shay' (to persist in something), when it continues and remains. Here there is a discussion: derived nouns (al-asmāʾ al-mushtaqqa) are the ones that are suitable to be described by them, whereas generic nouns (asmāʾ al-ajnās) are not used as descriptions, whether they are physical bodies or meanings. So one does not say "insān rajul jāʾa" (a human, a man, came), nor "lawn abyaḍ" (a color, white); rather one says "insān ʿālim" (a knowing human) and "jism abyaḍ" (a white body). Our saying "abyaḍ" means "a thing that has whiteness," and the body is not taken into it. This becomes clear in our saying "rajul ʿālim," for "ʿālim" is a thing that has knowledge, even a blacksmith or a baker; and if knowledge could subsist in them both, they would be knowing. The living (ḥayy) is not included in the meaning from the standpoint of concept, for when we say "ʿālim" it is understood that this is living; because the word was not established for a living thing that knows, rather the word was established for a thing that is known. This is made clearer by our saying "maʿlūm," for it is a thing that is known or a matter that is known, even if it is not a thing. If the body were included in "abyaḍ," our saying "jism abyaḍ" would be like our saying "jism lahu bayāḍ" (a body that has whiteness), and the description would fall upon the mass. Once you know this, from what is derived by the genus, some things are conveyed and others are not: our saying "al-Hindī" applies to everything attributed to India, but "al-muhannad" is a sword attributed to India, so it is correct to say "ʿabd Hindī" (an Indian slave) and "tamr Hindī" (Indian dates), but it is not correct to say "muhannad." Likewise "al-ablaq" (piebald) is a color in a horse, and one does not say of a garment "ablaq"; similarly "al-afṭas" is a nose that has a depression, so when one says of someone, "anf afṭas" (a flat nose), it is as if he said "anf bihi faṭas" (a nose with flatness in it), so it describes him with the mass. It should not be said "faras ablaq" (a piebald horse), "anf afṭas" (a flat nose), or "sayf muhannad" (an Indian sword), yet they say it. So what is the answer? This objection bears on ṣarṣar, for it is the cold wind. When one says "rīḥ ṣarṣar," that is not like our saying "rīḥ bāridah" (a cold wind), for ṣarṣar is simply the cold wind, so it is as if he said "rīḥ bāridah." We say: words whose meanings involve two or more things, like our saying "ʿālim," for it indicates a thing that has knowledge, so there is a thing and knowledge. They are of three categories.

The first: the state (al-ḥāl) is the intended thing and the locus (al-maḥall) is subordinate, as in ʿālim, ḍārib (one who strikes), and abyaḍ, for the intended things in these words are knowledge, striking, and whiteness specifically. As for the locus, it is intended insofar as it is in its generality, so that if whiteness were replaced by the color of something else, the intended meaning would be disrupted, as in aswad (black). As for the body which is the locus of whiteness, if it were possible to replace it, and if whiteness could subsist in a substance other than a body, the purpose would not be disrupted.

The second: the locus is the intended thing, as in our saying "al-ḥayawān" (the animal), for it is a name for the genus of that which has life, not like "ḥayy" (living), which is a name for a thing that has life. So here the intended thing is the locus, which is the body, such that if a living thing that is not a body were found, the aim of one who says "al-ḥayawān" would not be achieved. And if the word "ḥayawān" were applied to God, the Living who does not die, the speaker's purpose would be achieved; but if the word "ḥayawān" were applied to a standing horse or a sleeping human whom life has not left, the listener would gain nothing and the speaker would not achieve his purpose. For when one says of a person, who is standing while dead, "This is an animal," and then his death becomes evident, he does not retract what he said but says: "I did not say he is living; I said he is an animal, and he is an animal whom life has left."

The third: where both things are intended, as in our saying "rajul" (man), "imraʾah" (woman), "nāqah" (she-camel), and "jamal" (male camel). For "rajul" is a name established for a male human, "imraʾah" for a female human, "nāqah" for a female camel, and "jamal" for a male camel. So if "nāqah" is applied to an animal and it turns out to be a horse or a bull, the purpose is disrupted; likewise if it turns out to be a male camel. Once you know this, in every case where the locus was intended either alone or together with the state, it is not described by it. So one does not say "jism ḥayawān" (a living body) or "baʿīr nāqah" (a camel, a she-camel); rather that is made into a compound, and it is described by the compound, so one says "jism huwa ḥayawān" (a body which is an animal) and "baʿīr huwa nāqah" (a camel which is a she-camel). Then, the ablaq and the afṭas have a nature which is animal in one respect and knowing in another; likewise "muhannad." But the indication that the state is preferred in it is clear, because "muhannad" is mentioned only to praise the sword, and "afṭas" is said only to describe the nose, not as its essence; likewise "ablaq." In contrast, "ḥayawān" is not said for its description. Likewise "nāqah." Once you know this, ṣarṣar is said of the intensity of the wind or of its coldness, so it is required that what applies to the cold and the intense applies to it, and thus description is permissible. This is a precious discussion.

The third issue: He, exalted is He, said here: ﴿Indeed We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, and in al-Dhariyat He said: ﴿And in ʿĀd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 41]. So He defined "the wind" there and made it indefinite here, because barrenness in the wind is more evident than the cold that harms plants or the intensity that uproots trees. The barren wind is the one that neither produces clouds nor fertilizes trees, and it occurs frequently; whereas the destructive cold wind is rarely found. So He said "al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm" (the barren wind), meaning this well-known genus, then He added clarification with His saying: ﴿that leaves nothing it comes upon but makes it like the rotted remains﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 42], so it was distinguished from the barren wind. As for ṣarṣar, it occurs rarely, so it is not well known, and thus He made it indefinite.

The fourth issue: He said here ﴿on a day of misfortune continuous﴾, and in Fussilat He said: ﴿in days of misfortune﴾ [Fussilat: 16], and in al-Haqqah He said: ﴿seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. The meaning of "day" here is the time and period, as in His saying: ﴿the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 33]. His saying "mustamirr" (continuous) conveys what "days" conveys, because continuity indicates the passing of time, as "days" indicates it. The wording differs while the meaning is one because the narration here is given in summary: He mentioned the time but did not mention its duration, and for this reason He did not describe it.

Moreover, there are two readings in it. One is ﴿yawmi naḥsin﴾ with the genitive construction of "yawm," and the sukūn on naḥs on the pattern of nafs. The second is "yawmin naḥisin" with tanwīn on the mīm and kasra on the ḥāʾ, describing the day as "naḥis" (unlucky), as in His saying: ﴿in days of misfortune﴾. If it is said: which of the two is closer? We say: the genitive construction is more correct, because whoever reads "yawmin naḥisin mustamirrin" makes "mustamirr" an adjective of "yawm," whereas whoever reads "yawmi naḥsin mustamirrin" makes "mustamirr" an adjective of "naḥs," so there results the continuation of ill fortune. The first is more evident and more fitting. If it is said: whoever reads "yawmi naḥsin" with a sukūn on the ḥāʾ, what does he say about "naḥis"? We say: it may be said that it is a lightened form of "naḥs," like "fakhdh" and "fakhidh" outside of descriptions, and "naṣr" and "naṣir," "raʿd" and "raʿid." On this view he must say its underlying form is "yawmin kāʾinin naḥisin," as you say in His saying: ﴿on the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44]. And it may be said that "naḥis" is not an adjective but a noun of meaning or a verbal noun, so it is like the expression "yawm bard wa ḥarr" (a day of cold and heat), and this is closer and more correct.

The fifth issue: What is the meaning of "mustamirr"? We say: there are several aspects:

The first: extended, enduring for a long duration, from "istamarra al-amr" when it persisted. This is like His saying: ﴿in days of misfortune﴾, because the plural conveys the meaning of continuity and extension, and likewise His saying: ﴿in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7].

The second: severe, from "marrah" (a single time), as we said earlier concerning His saying: ﴿a continuous magic﴾ [al-Qamar: 2]. This is like the expression "days of hardships," and to it refers His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in days of misfortune, that We may make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾, for He makes them taste the bitter, harmful punishment.

**Issue one:** Is ﴿تَنْزِعُ النّاسَ﴾ (*tanziʿu an-nās*, "it uproots the people") a descriptive qualifier (*wasf*) or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action)? We say that it admits both possibilities, since it is correct to say "He sent a violent wind uprooting the people" and it is also correct to say "The wind was sent uprooting." If it is asked: how can it be a circumstantial clause when the entity it describes (*dhū al-ḥāl*) is indefinite (*nakira*)? We reply that the matter here is easier than in His saying, ﴿وَلَقَدْ جاءَهم مِنَ الأنْباءِ ما فِيهِ مُزْدَجَرٌ﴾ ("And there had certainly come to them of the reports that which contained a deterrent," Q. 54:4), where the noun is also indefinite. The answer given there is that *mā* is a qualified noun (*mawṣūfah*), so it is specified, and therefore it is acceptable to make it the entity of the circumstantial clause. Likewise we say: here the wind is qualified by *ṣarṣar* (violent, piercing), and the indefiniteness in it is for magnification. Otherwise it is in any case a three-part case, so it is not far-fetched to make it a circumstantial clause.

There is another possibility: that it is a resumptive sentence (*kalām mustaʾnaf*) built on a verb and subject, as when you say, "Zayd came, he pulled me." Its implied sense is "He came, so he pulled me." Likewise here He said, ﴿إنّا أرْسَلْنا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا﴾ ("Indeed, We sent upon them a wind," Q. 54:19), then ﴿فَأصْبَحَتْ تَنْزِعُ النّاسَ﴾ ("so it became uprooting the people"). This is supported by His saying, ﴿فَتَرى القَوْمَ فِيها صَرْعى﴾ ("So you see the people in it fallen prostrate," Q. 69:7). The *tāʾ* in *tanziʿu* refers back to what is indicated by *ṣarʿā* (fallen prostrate).

As for His saying, ﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾ ("as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees"), there are several interpretations.

First: It uprooted them and so felled them, ﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ﴾, as He said: ﴿صَرْعى كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ﴾ ("fallen prostrate as if they were trunks of palm trees," Q. 69:7).

Second: It uprooted them, and then they were, after the uprooting, ﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ﴾. This is closer, because *inqiʿār* (being uprooted at the base) comes before falling. It is as though the wind uproots the one person and tears him up, so he is uprooted and falls and becomes prostrate; then the place is emptied of him and becomes desolate (*yakhwā*). His saying in al-Ḥāqqah, ﴿فَتَرى القَوْمَ فِيها صَرْعى كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ خاوِيَةٍ﴾ ("So you see the people in it fallen prostrate as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees," Q. 69:7), refers to a state after *inqiʿār*, which itself comes after the uprooting. This indicates that the account here is abridged, since it does not mention their falling and the total emptiness of their dwellings. The condition of *inqiʿār* does not produce complete emptiness, because it is like the beginning of going out and taking up (the matter).

Third: It uproots them with violence, ﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ﴾, as though it were uprooting them so that they would be uprooted, as an indication of their strength and their firmness upon the earth. There are several meanings to this:
First: He mentioned this as an indication of the greatness of their bodies and the height of their stature.
Second: He mentioned it as an indication of their firmness in the earth; it is as though they were setting their feet in the earth and seeking to prevent the wind by it.
Third: He mentioned it as an indication of their dryness and desiccation by the wind; it was killing them and burning them with its extreme coldness, so they fell as though they were dry pieces of wood.

**Issue two:** He said here, ﴿مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾ (*munqaʿir*, masculine), so He made the palm masculine. In al-Ḥāqqah He said, ﴿كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ خاوِيَةٍ﴾ (*khāwiyah*, feminine). The exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*) said: in that surah the final verses required that, because of His saying, ﴿مُسْتَمِرٌّ﴾ (Q. 54:2), ﴿مُنْهَمِرٍ﴾ (Q. 54:11), and ﴿مُنْتَشِرٌ﴾ (Q. 54:7). This is a good answer, since speech is adorned by beauty of expression as it is by beauty of meaning. It is also possible to say: the word *nakhl* (palm) has the form of the singular, like *baql* (herbs) and *naml* (ants), while its meaning is that of the plural. So it is permissible to say of it: *nakhlun munqaʿirun*, *munqaʿirah*, and *munqaʿirāt*; *nakhlun khāwin*, *khāwiyah*, and *khāwiyāt*; *nakhlun bāsiqun*, *bāsiqah*, and *bāsiqāt*. When someone says *munqaʿir*, *khāwin*, or *bāsiq*, he has looked only at the form and has not attended to the aspect of meaning. When he says *munqaʿirāt*, *khāwiyāt*, or *bāsiqāt*, he has looked only at the meaning and has not attended to the aspect of form. When he says *munqaʿirah*, *khāwiyah*, or *bāsiqah*, he has combined both considerations, in terms of the unity of the word. Sometimes one says *munqaʿirah* in the singular in terms of form, and the feminine *tāʾ* that belongs to the plural is attached to it. Knowing this, we say: God, exalted is He, mentioned the word *nakhl* in three places and described it in the three ways. He said, ﴿وَالنَّخْلَ باسِقاتٍ﴾ ("and the palm trees towering high," Q. 50:10), where *bāsiqāt* is a circumstantial qualifier of it and functions as a description. He said, ﴿نَخْلٍ خاوِيَةٍ﴾ (Q. 69:7), and He said, ﴿نَخْلٍ مُنْقَعِرٍ﴾. Where He said *munqaʿir*, that was the preferred form, because *munqaʿir* in reality functions like a passive participle (*maf'ūl*), since it is the one upon which uprooting fell, so it is *maqʿūr* (uprooted). *Khāwī* and *bāsiq* are active participles (*fāʿil*), and their meaning is the emptying of that which is a passive participle of the feminine sign first, as you say: *imraʾatun kafīl* and *imraʾatun kafīlah*, and *imraʾatun kabīr* and *imraʾatun kabīrah*. As for *bāsiqāt*, these are active in reality, since towering height is a matter that subsisted in them. As for *khāwiyah*, it is of the type of the beauty of the aspect, since *khāwī* refers to its place; it is as if He said: palm trees whose places are empty. This is the utmost in inimitability (*iʿjāz*), in that He brought a word appropriate to the preceding and following words in terms of form. The proof therefore required this, unlike the poet who chooses a word according to a weak position for the sake of metre and rhyme.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verses 24–25:**

On His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *Zaydan darabtuhu* (زَيْدًا ضَرَبْتُهُ) and *Zaydun darbatuhu* (زَيْدٌ ضَرْبَتُهُ) are both permissible, but the accusative (naṣb) is preferred in certain positions, and this verse is one of them. This is the case where what follows the interrogative particle may take either the accusative or the nominative. The reason for preferring the accusative is intelligible: the questioner asks the one questioned to make what he mentions after the interrogative particle the subject (mubtada') of his speech, and to inform him about it. When one says *a-Zaydun 'indaka?* (أزَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ), its meaning is: "Inform me about Zayd and mention to me his condition." When a mentioned verb is added to this state, the accusative is favored, so one may say *a-Zaydan darabtahu?* (أزَيْدًا ضَرَبْتَهُ). Even if it is not obligatory, the accusative is the better choice. If it is said: "Why did the one who recited ﴿أبَشَرًا مِنّا واحِدًا نَتَّبِعُهُ﴾ abandon the better reading?" We answer: out of regard for His words, "they said" (فَقالُوا), since what follows "said" can only be a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and the nominal form is preferable, and the preferable is stronger and clearer.

[p. 45]

**The second issue:** If *basharan* (بَشَرًا) is in the accusative governed by a verb, what is the wisdom in the verb coming later in the surface structure? We answer: it has been stated many times that an eloquent speaker places first in speech what his purpose is most concerned with. They wanted to demonstrate that they were justified in refusing to follow him. Had they said: "Shall we follow a human being?" one could answer: "Yes, follow him, and what prevents you from following him?" But when they put his condition first and said: "He is one of our kind, a human being from our category, not a stranger whom we believe knows what we do not know or has power what we do not have, and he is a lone individual with no army, retinue, horses, or servants, so how can we follow him?" then they had put forward the reason that justifies refraining from following him. Know that in this verse there are indications of this:

First: They made him indefinite (nakira) when they said *basharan* (أبَشَرًا), and did not say: "Shall we follow a righteous man," or "the man claiming prophethood," or any other definite description. Indefiniteness indicates contempt.

Second: They said *basharan* and did not say *rajulan* (أرَجُلًا).

Third: They said *minna* (مِنّا, "from among us"). This carries two meanings:

The first: he is of our category, not a stranger.

The second: *minna* means "one who follows us." A speaker says to another, "You are one of us," and the listener is offended and replies, "No, rather you are one of us, and I am not one of you." The underlying point is that *min* (مِن) indicates partitiveness, and the part follows the whole, not the whole following the part.

Fourth: *wahidan* (واحِدًا) also carries two meanings:

The first: "lone," indicating his weakness.

The second: "single," meaning he is one of the common people (ahad), not one of the eminent, well-known notables. The explanation of using *aḥad* for the lowly, as in the expression "he is one of the people's *aḥad*," is this: whoever is not known for lineage or nobility, when someone who does not know him narrates from him, cannot say "So-and-so said" or "the son of so-and-so said." Instead he says, "A single man said, and a single man did," and this is the utmost obscurity, because no one attaches himself to the base, so he remains alone most of the time. Thus the base are called *aḥad*.

* *

As for His words concerning them: ﴿Indeed, we would then be in error and madness﴾, this may carry two meanings:

The first: they may have said this in reply to one who told them: "If you do not follow him, you will be in error." They replied to him: "No, rather if we follow him, we will be in error."

The second: that this is a sequence on what preceded, meaning his condition is as we have mentioned, weakness and loneliness, so if we follow him, we will be in error and madness (su'r), that is, insanity, on this interpretation. If we say that they said this as a reply, then the speaker would have said to them: "If you do not follow him, then we are now in error, and in the hereafter in madness (sa'ir)." They replied: "No, rather if we followed him, we would now be in error and in madness, meaning in the sense of humiliation and servitude, figuratively, since they did not acknowledge the Blaze (sa'ir)."

**The third issue:** The Blaze (al-sa'ir) in the hereafter is singular, so why is it expressed in the plural (su'ur)? We answer: the response to this is from several aspects:

First: In Jahannam there are levels (darakat), and it is possible that each one is a blaze, or that there is a blaze within them.

Second: Because the punishment is continuous upon them. Whenever their skins are roasted, He replaces them with other skins, so it is as if they are in a different blaze and a different punishment at every moment.

Third: Because of the vastness of the single Blaze, it is as if it were blazes. One says of a single man: "So-and-so is not a single man, but he is men."

Then He, exalted is He, said concerning them:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us? Rather, he is an arch-liar, insolent.﴾ It has been stated that negation by way of interrogation is more emphatic, because one who says, "Nothing has been revealed to him," perhaps knows or suspects or imagines that the listener disbelieves him in it. But when it is expressed by way of interrogation, its meaning is that the listener answers him by saying, "Nothing has been sent down," so the matter becomes then a negation that is evident and hidden from no one. Rather, everyone says, "Nothing has been sent down." The Reminder (al-dhikr) means the message or the Book, if it existed. It may also be intended to mean what he mentions from God, exalted is He, just as one says "the truth" (al-haqq) and means what descends from God. On this there are issues:

[p. 46]

**The first issue:** Their saying *a-ulqiya* (أأُلْقِيَ, "has it been cast down") replaces *a-unzila* (أأُنْزِلَ, "has it been sent down"). In this there is an indication of what they denied, by way of exaggeration. This is because casting down (al-ilqa') is descending swiftly, and the Prophet used to say: "The revelation came to me with the angel in a brief moment." So it is as if they said: "The angel is a body, and the heaven is far away, so how can he descend in a moment?" Therefore they said *ulqiya* and did not say *unzila*. Their saying "upon him" ('alayhi) is another denial, as if they said: "No reminder has been cast down at all. If it has been cast down, it is not upon him from among us, when among us there is one who is above him in nobility and intelligence." Their saying *a-ulqiya* in place of *a-alqa Allahu* (أألْقى اللَّهُ) is to indicate that casting down from heaven is not possible, let alone from God, exalted is He.

**The second issue:** They named the Reminder (al-dhikr) definitely and did not say "has a reminder been cast down upon him." This is because God, exalted is He, related their denial of what should not be denied, and said: "They denied the manifest, clear Reminder, which should not be denied." So it is like the saying of one who says, "They denied the known."

**The third issue:** *Bal* (بَلْ, "rather") requires a matter previously set aside. What is that? We answer: their saying *a-ulqiya* is for denial, as they said: "Nothing has been cast down." Then their saying "has the Reminder been cast down upon him" only implies that he is not a prophet. Then they said: "Rather, he is not truthful."

**The fourth issue:** *Al-kadhdhab* (الكَذّابُ) is an intensive form (fa''al) from *fa'il* for intensification. Or is it said that *bal* is from *fa'il* like *khayyat* (tailor) and *tamma*r (date-seller)? We answer: the first is the correct and more apparent, while the second is of the same kind (in meaning), because one who is attributed to something must practice it frequently. Whoever sews his garment once is not called a tailor. Knowing this, we say: intensification is either in quantity or in intensity. So *al-kadhdhab* is either one who lies intensely, saying what reason does not accept, or one who lies very frequently. It is possible that they described him with it because they believed both of these about him. Their saying *ashir* (أشِرٌ, "insolent") indicates that he lies not out of necessity or need for deliverance, as the weak person lies. Rather, he has become self-sufficient and arrogant and sought leadership over you, and wanted you to follow him. So every attribute was a barrier to following him, because the liar is not heeded, especially when his lying is not out of necessity. It is recited as *ashharru* (أشَرُّ). The exegetes said: this is on the rejected original form of *ashir*, and the latter is in the pattern of the elative (af'al al-tafdil). The original form was abandoned because when *af'al* is explained, it may be explained by *af'al* again, and the second by a third *af'al*. For example, if one asks, "What is the meaning of *al-a'lam* (the most knowledgeable)?" it is said: "He is the one with more knowledge." But if it is asked, "More of what?" it is said: "More in number," or "a thing like it." Therefore there must be a matter by which the forms are explained, not from its own pattern. So they said: the elative form, and virtue (fadila) originally comes from goodness (khayr), and goodness is the root in the pattern of *af'al*, so one does not say *akhyar*. Then, since evil (sharr) is the opposite of good, it is treated as good is treated: one says "he is evil compared to so-and-so" and "he is good compared to so-and-so," and *ashirr* is the opposite of *akhyar*. Then *khayr* is used in two places:

The first: the intensification of goodness by a verb or by *af'al*, depending on the variant. One says, "This is good" and "This is better" (akhyar), and it is used in intensifying *khayr* by resemblance, not on the original basis. So whoever says *ashirr* has abandoned the used original, because it was taken from the rejected original with the meaning "he is evil compared to others." Likewise the meaning of *al-a'lam* is that his knowledge is better than the knowledge of others, or that he is better than the heedlessness of ignorance. The same applies to *al-ad'af* (the weakest) and other such forms.

We answer: out of regard for His words, "they said" (فَقالُوا), since what follows "said" can only be a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and the nominal form is preferable, and the preferable is stronger and clearer.

[p. 45]

**The second issue:** If *basharan* (بَشَرًا) is in the accusative governed by a verb, what is the wisdom in the verb coming later in the surface structure? We answer: it has been stated many times that an eloquent speaker places first in speech what his purpose is most concerned with. They wanted to demonstrate that they were justified in refusing to follow him. Had they said: "Shall we follow a human being?" one could answer: "Yes, follow him, and what prevents you from following him?" But when they put his condition first and said: "He is one of our kind, a human being from our category, not a stranger whom we believe knows what we do not know or has power what we do not have, and he is a lone individual with no army, retinue, horses, or servants, so how can we follow him?" then they had put forward the reason that justifies refraining from following him. Know that in this verse there are indications of this:

First: They made him indefinite (nakira) when they said *basharan* (أبَشَرًا), and did not say: "Shall we follow a righteous man," or "the man claiming prophethood," or any other definite description. Indefiniteness indicates contempt.

Second: They said *basharan* and did not say *rajulan* (أرَجُلًا).

Third: They said *minna* (مِنّا, "from among us"). This carries two meanings:

The first: he is of our category, not a stranger.

The second: *minna* means "one who follows us." A speaker says to another, "You are one of us," and the listener is offended and replies, "No, rather you are one of us, and I am not one of you." The underlying point is that *min* (مِن) indicates partitiveness, and the part follows the whole, not the whole following the part.

Fourth: *wahidan* (واحِدًا) also carries two meanings:

The first: "lone," indicating his weakness.

The second: "single," meaning he is one of the common people (ahad), not one of the eminent, well-known notables. The explanation of using *aḥad* for the lowly, as in the expression "he is one of the people's *aḥad*," is this: whoever is not known for lineage or nobility, when someone who does not know him narrates from him, cannot say "So-and-so said" or "the son of so-and-so said." Instead he says, "A single man said, and a single man did," and this is the utmost obscurity, because no one attaches himself to the base, so he remains alone most of the time. Thus the base are called *aḥad*.

As for His words concerning them: ﴿Indeed, we would then be in error and madness﴾, this may carry two meanings:

The first: they may have said this in reply to one who told them: "If you do not follow him, you will be in error." They replied to him: "No, rather if we follow him, we will be in error."

The second: that this is a sequence on what preceded, meaning his condition is as we have mentioned, weakness and loneliness, so if we follow him, we will be in error and madness (su'r), that is, insanity, on this interpretation. If we say that they said this as a reply, then the speaker would have said to them: "If you do not follow him, then we are now in error, and in the hereafter in madness (sa'ir)." They replied: "No, rather if we followed him, we would now be in error and in madness, meaning in the sense of humiliation and servitude, figuratively, since they did not acknowledge the Blaze (sa'ir)."

**The third issue:** The Blaze (al-sa'ir) in the hereafter is singular, so why is it expressed in the plural (su'ur)? We answer: the response to this is from several aspects:

First: In Jahannam there are levels (darakat), and it is possible that each one is a blaze, or that there is a blaze within them.

Second: Because the punishment is continuous upon them. Whenever their skins are roasted, He replaces them with other skins, so it is as if they are in a different blaze and a different punishment at every moment.

Third: Because of the vastness of the single Blaze, it is as if it were blazes. One says of a single man: "So-and-so is not a single man, but he is men."

Then He, exalted is He, said concerning them:

Rather, he is an arch-liar, insolent.﴾ It has been stated that negation by way of interrogation is more emphatic, because one who says, "Nothing has been revealed to him," perhaps knows or suspects or imagines that the listener disbelieves him in it. But when it is expressed by way of interrogation, its meaning is that the listener answers him by saying, "Nothing has been sent down," so the matter becomes then a negation that is evident and hidden from no one. Rather, everyone says, "Nothing has been sent down." The Reminder (al-dhikr) means the message or the Book, if it existed. It may also be intended to mean what he mentions from God, exalted is He, just as one says "the truth" (al-haqq) and means what descends from God. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** Their saying *a-ulqiya* (أأُلْقِيَ, "has it been cast down") replaces *a-unzila* (أأُنْزِلَ, "has it been sent down"). In this there is an indication of what they denied, by way of exaggeration. This is because casting down (al-ilqa') is descending swiftly, and the Prophet used to say: "The revelation came to me with the angel in a brief moment." So it is as if they said: "The angel is a body, and the heaven is far away, so how can he descend in a moment?" Therefore they said *ulqiya* and did not say *unzila*. Their saying "upon him" ('alayhi) is another denial, as if they said: "No reminder has been cast down at all. If it has been cast down, it is not upon him from among us, when among us there is one who is above him in nobility and intelligence." Their saying *a-ulqiya* in place of *a-alqa Allahu* (أألْقى اللَّهُ) is to indicate that casting down from heaven is not possible, let alone from God, exalted is He.

**The second issue:** They named the Reminder (al-dhikr) definitely and did not say "has a reminder been cast down upon him." This is because God, exalted is He, related their denial of what should not be denied, and said: "They denied the manifest, clear Reminder, which should not be denied." So it is like the saying of one who says, "They denied the known."

**The third issue:** *Bal* (بَلْ, "rather") requires a matter previously set aside. What is that? We answer: their saying *a-ulqiya* is for denial, as they said: "Nothing has been cast down." Then their saying "has the Reminder been cast down upon him" only implies that he is not a prophet. Then they said: "Rather, he is not truthful."

**The fourth issue:** *Al-kadhdhab* (الكَذّابُ) is an intensive form (fa''al) from *fa'il* for intensification. Or is it said that *bal* is from *fa'il* like *khayyat* (tailor) and *tamma*r (date-seller)? We answer: the first is the correct and more apparent, while the second is of the same kind (in meaning), because one who is attributed to something must practice it frequently. Whoever sews his garment once is not called a tailor. Knowing this, we say: intensification is either in quantity or in intensity. So *al-kadhdhab* is either one who lies intensely, saying what reason does not accept, or one who lies very frequently. It is possible that they described him with it because they believed both of these about him. Their saying *ashir* (أشِرٌ, "insolent") indicates that he lies not out of necessity or need for deliverance, as the weak person lies. Rather, he has become self-sufficient and arrogant and sought leadership over you, and wanted you to follow him. So every attribute was a barrier to following him, because the liar is not heeded, especially when his lying is not out of necessity. It is recited as *ashharru* (أشَرُّ). The exegetes said: this is on the rejected original form of *ashir*, and the latter is in the pattern of the elative (af'al al-tafdil). The original form was abandoned because when *af'al* is explained, it may be explained by *af'al* again, and the second by a third *af'al*. For example, if one asks, "What is the meaning of *al-a'lam* (the most knowledgeable)?" it is said: "He is the one with more knowledge." But if it is asked, "More of what?" it is said: "More in number," or "a thing like it." Therefore there must be a matter by which the forms are explained, not from its own pattern. So they said: the elative form, and virtue (fadila) originally comes from goodness (khayr), and goodness is the root in the pattern of *af'al*, so one does not say *akhyar*. Then, since evil (sharr) is the opposite of good, it is treated as good is treated: one says "he is evil compared to so-and-so" and "he is good compared to so-and-so," and *ashirr* is the opposite of *akhyar*. Then *khayr* is used in two places:

The first: the intensification of goodness by a verb or by *af'al*, depending on the variant. One says, "This is good" and "This is better" (akhyar), and it is used in intensifying *khayr* by resemblance, not on the original basis. So whoever says *ashirr* has abandoned the used original, because it was taken from the rejected original with the meaning "he is evil compared to others." Likewise the meaning of *al-a'lam* is that his knowledge is better than the knowledge of others, or that he is better than the heedlessness of ignorance. The same applies to *al-ad'af* (the weakest) and other such forms.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one.﴾ If someone says: "sa-ya'lamu" (they will know) refers to the future, yet at the time the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) they already knew, because after death matters become clear, and they had witnessed what they witnessed. So how is this to be understood?

We say: there are two aspects to this.

The first: this statement is to be understood as occurring at the time of their saying, "Rather, he is a liar, insolent." It is as if Allah the Exalted said, on the day they said, "Rather, he is a liar, insolent": ﴿They will know tomorrow﴾.

The second: this threat is of punishment, not of the attainment of knowledge of the painful punishment, which is the punishment of Hell and not the punishment of the grave. They will be punished on the Day of Resurrection, which is in the future. His saying, ﴿tomorrow﴾, is due to the nearness of the time in both possibility and perception. Then, if we say that this is a threat of punishment and not a refutation, there is no need to explain it further; rather, it is a repetition of their statement without intending its meaning. And if we say that it is a rebuttal and a promise by explaining the disclosure of the matter, then His saying, ﴿They will know tomorrow﴾, means: they will know tomorrow that they are the liars who denied, not out of need or necessity, but they were insolent and arrogant when they became self-sufficient. His saying, ﴿tomorrow﴾, may mean the Day of Resurrection, and it may mean the Day of Punishment. This is according to the first aspect.

If it is objected that His saying ﴿then they called [to their companion]﴾ is evidence that the intended meaning is the past, we answer: we will respond to that in its proper place.

As for the distinction, we say: the narration of Thamud is given in full detail in this passage, where He mentioned the people's denial of the warner, their saying to their messenger, and the confirmation of the messengers in His saying ﴿They will know﴾. He mentioned the miracle, which is the she-camel, what they did to it, the punishment and the destruction. He recounts the narrative in both the past and future manner so that its description for the Prophet (ﷺ) is as though he were present with it, so that he would follow Salih in patience and in calling to the truth, and would trust in his Lord for victory over the enemies with the truth. So He said: "Indeed, I support you with a decisive miracle."

Know that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned five stories in this surah, and He made the middle story mentioned in the most complete way, because the condition of Salih was most similar to the condition of Muhammad (ﷺ). For he brought an astonishing, earthly sign, more wondrous than what the prophets brought. For ʿIsa (peace be upon him) brought the dead to life, but the dead man was a receptacle for life, so he established life, by Allah's permission, in a place that was receptive to it. And Musa (peace be upon him) had his staff turn into a serpent, so Allah established life in the wood. But the wood is a plant that has a power of growth, resembling an animal in its growth, so it is more wondrous. And Salih (peace be upon him) had apparent in his hand the emergence of the she-camel from the rock: an inanimate object, with no capacity for life and no capacity for growth in it. And the Prophet (ﷺ) brought something more wondrous than all of these, which is the manipulation of the body of the heavens, which the polytheist says no one can reach the heaven, nor is it possible to split or pierce it. As for the earthly bodies, they said that they are substances sharing the same matter, each of which can accept the form of the other, while the heavens do not accept that. So when he brought what they knew no human could produce the like of, it was more complete and more eloquent than the miracle of Salih (peace be upon him), which is the most complete miracle among the miracles of prophets other than Muhammad (ﷺ).

(And here is a subtle point.) When the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the agent noun) is in the past sense and its object is mentioned with it, then the construct form (idafa) is required. You say: "Wahshi, the slayer of the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ)" [qatilu ʿammi]. If we say qatilun ʿamma al-nabiyyi with the operative form (i'mal), then it is necessary to assume the narration of a present state, as in His saying ﴿and their dog stretching out its forelegs﴾ [al-Kahf: 18], on the basis that it narrates the story as it happened. You say: "I went out yesterday, and behold, Zayd is striking ʿAmr," just as you say "he strikes ʿAmr," even if the striking has already occurred.

When it is in the future sense, the better form is the operative form (i'mal). You say: "Indeed, I will strike ʿAmr tomorrow." If you say "Indeed, I am the striker of ʿAmr tomorrow," it is permissible since the matter has occurred, but it is not the better form. The verification of this is that our saying "ḍarib" (striker), "sariq" (thief), and "qatil" (slayer) are in reality nouns, though they indicate the act. So when the act has been realized in the past, it has in reality ceased to exist, so the act has no existence in reality or in expectation. Therefore one must apply to the noun what belongs to it of the idafa, and leave aside what belongs to the verb of operation (i'mal), because of the predominance of nominality and the loss of the verb's past. But when the act is present or expected in the future, it has existence in reality or in expectation. Thus the idafa is permissible for the form of the noun, and the operative form is permissible for the expectation or existence of the act. However, the operative form is preferable, because in the future, "lan yadriba" (he will not strike) conveys "lā yakūnu ḍāriban" (he will not be a striker), so it should not be made an idafa. As for the operative form, it indicates the expectation or existence of the act, because when he says "Zayd is striking ʿAmr," the listener who hears of the striking of ʿAmr knows that he is doing it, and if he does not see it at the moment, he expects it in the future. However, the idafa gives lightness, since by it the tanwin and the nun are dropped, so one chooses the form for lightness of wording, not meaning.

Having understood this, we say: ﴿mursilu al-naqah﴾, with the lightness it has, implies the verification of the matter, and its assumption is as if it has occurred and existed, unlike if it were said "Indeed, We send the she-camel."

**The second issue:** "Fitnatan" (as a trial) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), so the trial is the aim of the sending. But the aim of it is the confirmation of the Prophet (ﷺ), who is Salih (peace be upon him), since it is a miracle. So what is the verified interpretation of this? We say there are two views:

The first: the miracle is a trial, because through it the condition of the one who will be rewarded is distinguished from the one who will be punished. For Allah, the Exalted, does not punish the unbelievers through the miracle except when it informs them of his truthfulness regarding his prophethood. So the miracle is a test, because it is a confirmation, and after the confirmation the one who confirms is distinguished from the one who denies.

The second, which is more subtle: the bringing forth of the she-camel from the rock was a miracle, while sending it to them, its roaming among them, and the division of water were a trial. For this reason He said ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a trial﴾ and did not say "Indeed, We are bringing out the she-camel as a trial." The verification of trial, testing, and examination has been discussed repeatedly before, and there is a subtle allusion to it, which is that Allah, the Exalted, guides whom He wills, and guidance has ways. Among them is what occurs in a manner in which the human has a role through acquisition (kasb): for example, He creates a sign that points, and the human's reflection and consideration of it occurs in a manner in which the truth becomes preponderant for him, so he follows it. And at other times He compels him to it from the outset and preserves him from error from his childhood. So the manifestation of the miraculous at the hand of the messenger is a matter through which He guides whom He wills to guidance along with acquisition. And the guidance of the prophets is without acquisition on their part; rather He creates in them knowledge that is not acquired. So His saying ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel as a trial﴾ is an allusion to them. For this reason He said to them [i.e., the Thamudites]. Its meaning is in a manner suitable for being a trial. And on this basis, whoever's miracle is more manifest, the reward of his people will be less.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so watch them﴾, means: watch them for the punishment. He did not say "watch for the punishment," as an allusion to the goodness of manners and avoidance of seeking evil. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and be patient﴾ supports this in the sense: if they harm you, do not hasten the punishment for them. It is also possible that this is an allusion to the nearness of the time of His command, and the matter is such that one is unable to be patient.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed We sent upon them a single shout, so they became like the dried branches of the one who builds a pen.﴾ They heard a shout and they died. In this there are issues:

The first issue: In His saying "fa-kānū" (so they became), what category is it? We say: the grammarians said: it sometimes comes with the meaning of "ṣāra" (to become), and they relied on the saying of a poet:

Then God the Exalted said: "And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will take heed?" (54:32). The repetition is for the sake of reminding.

Then He described the state of another people, namely the people of Lot, and said: "The people of Lot denied the warnings" (54:33).

Then He described their punishment and destruction, and said: "Indeed, We sent against them a squall of stones, except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn" (54:34). In this verse there are several issues:

The first: "ḥāṣib" (a squall, i.e., one who pelts) is an active participle from "ḥaṣaba," meaning he threw pebbles (ḥaṣbāʾ), and ḥaṣbāʾ is a name for stones. The thing sent against them is the stones themselves. God the Exalted said: "And We rained upon them stones of baked clay" (Hijr 15:74), and God the Exalted said concerning the angels: "to send upon them stones of clay" (Dhariyat 51:33). So what is sent against them is not "ḥāṣib." How is this answered? We say the answer has several aspects:

The first: We sent against them a wind that pelts with the stones, which are the pebbles, and the use of "ḥāṣib" for a violent wind became common, so the attribute was placed in the position of the thing described. If it is said: this is weak both in wording and in meaning. As for the wording, the wind is feminine, as God the Exalted said: "with a furious, violent wind" (Haqqah 69:6), "with a good wind" (Yunus 10:22), and God the Exalted said: "So We subjected the wind to him, running by his command" (Sad 38:36), and God the Exalted said: "its morning course was a month's journey" (Saba 34:12), and God the Exalted said concerning: "And We sent the winds fertilizing" (Hijr 15:22), and He did not say "liqāḥan" nor "liqḥah." As for the meaning, God the Exalted has explained that He sent upon them stones of baked clay, each marked with the sign of its own target, and these are not called pebbles; and that was by the hands of the angels, not by the wind. We say: the feminine gender of the wind is not real, and it has kinds of which the masculine predominates, like the whirlwind (iʿṣār). God the Exalted said: "then it was struck by a whirlwind containing fire" (Baqarah 2:266). So when it was a squall of stones, it was like that which contains fire. As for his saying that the throwing was with baked clay and not with pebbles, and by the hands of the angels and not by the wind, we say: every wind that throws stones is called "ḥāṣib." And how not, when the cloud that brings hail is called, by way of likening hail to pebbles, [a ḥāṣib]; so how would it not be said of the baked clay? As for the angels, they set the wind in motion, and it was the one that pelted the stones upon them.

The second answer: the meaning is a punishment that is a squall, and this is closer, since it includes the angel, the reckoning, the wind, and everything that may be supposed.

The third answer: His saying "ḥāṣiban" is closer than all of these, because His saying "Indeed We sent" indicates a sender, who is the sender of the stones and their squall. If it is said: he should have said "ḥāṣibīn" (masculine plural), we say: since he did not mention the described noun, he gave preference to the side of the wording, as if he had said "a thing squalling"; for the intended matter is to explain the kind of punishment, not to explain who the punishment was delivered by. Then it is said: we have no knowledge of it, and You alone are the Knowing, so inform us; and He said: "Indeed, We sent..."

We will explain this in the surah of al-Rahman.

The fourth issue: "illā āla Lūṭ" (except the family of Lot) is an exception from what? The answer to this is from two aspects:

One: the exception is from those to whom the pronoun in "against them" returns, namely the whole people, but His saying "The people of Lot denied" does not necessitate that his family were deniers, because the saying of one who says "the people of such-and-such a town disobeyed" is correct even if there were a small group in it who obeyed, how much more when there is among them only one or two obedient persons! If it is said: there is no need for the exception, because His saying "Indeed We sent against them" is correct even if a small group escaped from them, we say: since the benefit is only achieved by clarifying the destruction of those who denied and the rescue of those who believed, the mention of the rescue was intended; and where a small part of a large group is intended, it is not permissible to generalize and to speak absolutely without clarifying the state of that intended part by an exception or by a separate statement. Example: "So the angels prostrated, all of them together, except Iblis" (Hijr 15:30–31): He excepted the one because he was intended. And He said: "She was given of everything" (Naml 27:23) and did not make an exception, since the intent is to explain that she was given, not to explain that she was not given. In the narrative of Iblis both are intended, so that one knows that whoever is proud toward Adam is punished, and whoever is humble is rewarded; likewise the saying here. As for the denial, the intent seems to be mentioning the deniers, so no exception was made.

The second answer: the exception is from an implied statement, as if He had said: "Indeed We sent against them a squall, and We did not save anyone from the squall except the family of Lot." If it is said: when the exception is not from the people of Lot but from a general matter, must Lot also be excepted? We say: he is excepted by reason, because it is known that it is not permissible to leave him and to save his followers; and what shows that he is excepted is His saying, concerning the angels, in their answer to Abraham (peace be upon him) when he said: "Indeed Lot is in it": "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family, except his wife" (ʿAnkabut 29:32). The answer is like what we mentioned: one answer is that We sent to a people of whom it is truly said that they are criminals, even if some among them did not commit crime. The second: to a people who are criminals, with a destruction that encompasses all except the family of Lot. His saying: "We saved them at dawn" is a resumed statement, to explain the time of the rescue, or to explain the manner of the exception; for the family of Lot could have been among them and not been struck by the squall, as in ʿAd, where the wind uprooted the unbeliever and did no harm to the believer, or it made for them a means of escape, as in the people of Noah. So He said: "We saved them at dawn," that is, We commanded them to leave the town in the last part of the night. The "saḥar" is just before dawn, and it is said: it is the last sixth of the night.

The second answer: the exception is from an implied statement, as if He had said: "Indeed We sent against them a squall, and We did not save anyone from the squall except the family of Lot." And it is permissible that the sending against them and the destruction be general, as in His saying: "And guard against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong" (Anfal 8:25). So the squall destroyed everyone against whom the sending was intended, and those who were not so intended, such as their children, their animals and their dwellings; and none of them was saved except the family of Lot. If it is said: when the exception is not from the people of Lot but from a general matter, must Lot also be excepted? We say: he is excepted by reason, because it is known that it is not permissible to leave him and to save his followers; and what shows that he is excepted is His saying, concerning the angels, in their answer to Abraham (peace be upon him) when he said: "Indeed Lot is in it": "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family, except his wife" (ʿAnkabut 29:32). If it is said that His saying in Surah al-Hijr: "except the family of Lot; indeed we will surely save them" (Hijr 15:59) is an exception from the criminals, while the family of Lot were not criminals, so how was it excepted from them? The answer is like what we mentioned: one answer is that We sent to a people of whom it is truly said that they are criminals, even if some among them did not commit crime. The second: to a people who are criminals, with a destruction that encompasses all except the family of Lot. His saying: "We saved them at dawn" is a resumed statement, to explain the time of the rescue, or to explain the manner of the exception; for the family of Lot could have been among them and not been struck by the squall, as in ʿAd, where the wind uprooted the unbeliever and did no harm to the believer, or it made for them a means of escape, as in the people of Noah. So He said: "We saved them at dawn," that is, We commanded them to leave the town in the last part of the night. The "saḥar" is just before dawn, and it is said: it is the last sixth of the night.

Then God the Exalted said: "And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will take heed?" (54:32). The repetition is for the sake of reminding.

Then He described the state of another people, namely the people of Lot, and said: "The people of Lot denied the warnings" (54:33).

Then He described their punishment and destruction, and said: "Indeed, We sent against them a squall of stones, except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn" (54:34). In this verse there are several issues:

The first: "ḥāṣib" (a squall, i.e., one who pelts) is an active participle from "ḥaṣaba," meaning he threw pebbles (ḥaṣbāʾ), and ḥaṣbāʾ is a name for stones. The thing sent against them is the stones themselves. God the Exalted said: "And We rained upon them stones of baked clay" (Hijr 15:74), and God the Exalted said concerning the angels: "to send upon them stones of clay" (Dhariyat 51:33). So what is sent against them is not "ḥāṣib." How is this answered? We say the answer has several aspects:

The first: We sent against them a wind that pelts with the stones, which are the pebbles, and the use of "ḥāṣib" for a violent wind became common, so the attribute was placed in the position of the thing described. If it is said: this is weak both in wording and in meaning. As for the wording, the wind is feminine, as God the Exalted said: "with a furious, violent wind" (Haqqah 69:6), "with a good wind" (Yunus 10:22), and God the Exalted said: "So We subjected the wind to him, running by his command" (Sad 38:36), and God the Exalted said: "its morning course was a month's journey" (Saba 34:12), and God the Exalted said concerning: "And We sent the winds fertilizing" (Hijr 15:22), and He did not say "liqāḥan" nor "liqḥah." As for the meaning, God the Exalted has explained that He sent upon them stones of baked clay, each marked with the sign of its own target, and these are not called pebbles; and that was by the hands of the angels, not by the wind. We say: the feminine gender of the wind is not real, and it has kinds of which the masculine predominates, like the whirlwind (iʿṣār). God the Exalted said: "then it was struck by a whirlwind containing fire" (Baqarah 2:266). So when it was a squall of stones, it was like that which contains fire. As for his saying that the throwing was with baked clay and not with pebbles, and by the hands of the angels and not by the wind, we say: every wind that throws stones is called "ḥāṣib." And how not, when the cloud that brings hail is called, by way of likening hail to pebbles, [a ḥāṣib]; so how would it not be said of the baked clay? As for the angels, they set the wind in motion, and it was the one that pelted the stones upon them.

The second answer: the meaning is a punishment that is a squall, and this is closer, since it includes the angel, the reckoning, the wind, and everything that may be supposed.

The third answer: His saying "ḥāṣiban" is closer than all of these, because His saying "Indeed We sent" indicates a sender, who is the sender of the stones and their squall. If it is said: he should have said "ḥāṣibīn" (masculine plural), we say: since he did not mention the described noun, he gave preference to the side of the wording, as if he had said "a thing squalling"; for the intended matter is to explain the kind of punishment, not to explain who the punishment was delivered by. This applies against the one who says "the wind is feminine," because omitting the feminine marker there is like omitting the plural marker here.

The second issue: He linked the sending to the denial with the particle "fa" (so), but He did not say "The people of Lot denied the warnings, so We sent," as in the phrase: "So We opened the gates of heaven" (Qamar 54:11), because the narrative is laid out in the manner of the narratives mentioned before, as if He had said: "So how was My punishment and My warnings?" as He said before. Then it is said: we have no knowledge of it, and You alone are the Knowing, so inform us; and He said: "Indeed, We sent..."

The third issue: What is the wisdom in omitting the phrase "So how was My punishment," where He did not say "So how was My punishment," as He said in the three narratives? We say: because repetition three times is sufficient, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Have I not conveyed [the message]? (three times)," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Her marriage is void, void, void." The reminder was repeated three times, so emphasis was achieved by three repetitions. We have explained that He mentioned "So how was My punishment" in the narrative of Noah for magnification, in the narrative of Thamud for clarification, and in the narrative of ʿAd He repeated it twice for both magnification and clarification together. Know that He mentioned "So how was My punishment" in three narratives four times; the single occurrence is for warning, and the three occurrences are for reminding, because the purpose was achieved by the single occurrence. His saying: "Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" (Rahman 55) He mentioned once for clarification and repeated it thirty times besides the first occurrence, just as He repeated "So how was My punishment and My warnings" three times besides the first occurrence. So the mention of the favours was ten times the mention of the punishment, pointing to the mercy about which He said: "Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like of it, and whoever brings an evil deed will be recompensed only with its like" (An'am 6:160). We will explain this in the surah of al-Rahman.

The fourth issue: "illā āla Lūṭ" (except the family of Lot) is an exception from what? If it is from those of whom He said "Indeed We sent against them a squall," then the pronoun in "against them" refers to the people of Lot, and they are those of whom He said "The people of Lot denied"; then He said "Indeed We sent against them." But He made no exception at His saying "The people of Lot denied," and his family are from his people, so would his family have denied, which was not the case? The answer to this is from two aspects:

One: the exception is from those to whom the pronoun in "against them" returns, namely the whole people, but His saying "The people of Lot denied" does not necessitate that his family were deniers, because the saying of one who says "the people of such-and-such a town disobeyed" is correct even if there were a small group in it who obeyed, how much more when there is among them only one or two obedient persons! If it is said: there is no need for the exception, because His saying "Indeed We sent against them" is correct even if a small group escaped from them, we say: since the benefit is only achieved by clarifying the destruction of those who denied and the rescue of those who believed, the mention of the rescue was intended; and where a small part of a large group is intended, it is not permissible to generalize and to speak absolutely without clarifying the state of that intended part by an exception or by a separate statement. Example: "So the angels prostrated, all of them together, except Iblis" (Hijr 15:30–31): He excepted the one because he was intended. And He said: "She was given of everything" (Naml 27:23) and did not make an exception, since the intent is to explain that she was given, not to explain that she was not given. Then God Most High said: ﴿A blessing from Us. Thus do We reward whoever gives thanks.﴾ That is, that deliverance was a favour from Us, just as that destruction was justice; and had they been destroyed, that too would have been justice. God Most High said: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have done wrong.﴾ [al-Anfal: 25] The wise men said: a corrupt limb is cut off, and some of the sound part must necessarily be cut off with it so that the corruption may be completely eradicated. However, God Most High is capable of perfect distinction; He is free to choose. If He wills, He destroys both those who believed and those who denied, and then He grants firm standing in the abode of recompense to those among the believers whom He destroyed. And if He wills, He destroys only the one who denied. So He said: ﴿A blessing from Us﴾, pointing to that, and in its accusative (naṣb) there are two possibilities:

The first: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), as if He had said: We delivered them as a blessing from Us.

The second: it is an infinitive (maṣdar), since deliverance from Him is a bestowal of favour; so it is as if God Most High had said: We bestowed upon them a favour by the deliverance.

As for His words ﴿Thus do We reward whoever gives thanks﴾, there are two possibilities concerning it.

The first, which is apparent and which most exegetes hold, is that whoever believes, We thus deliver him from the punishment of this world and do not destroy him, a promise to the believing community of Muhammad ﷺ that He will protect them from general destructions and all-encompassing, comprehensive calamities.

The second, and it is the more correct, is that this is a promise to them, and their recompense is reward in the Hereafter, as if He had said: just as We delivered them in this world, so We will bestow favour upon them on the Day of Reckoning. What supports this is that deliverance from destructions in this world is not necessary, whereas deliverance from the punishment of God in the Hereafter is necessary by the ruling of the threat. Likewise God delivers the thankful from the punishment of the Fire and leaves the wrongdoers in it. This is indicated by His words: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, We give him of it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him of it; and We will reward the thankful.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145] And His words: ﴿So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the recompense of the good-doers.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 85] The thankful person is a good-doer, so it is known that what is meant is their recompense in the Hereafter.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And he had warned them of Our assault, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ In this there is a clearing of Lut, peace be upon him, and a declaration that he had fulfilled what was incumbent upon him. For when God Most High linked punishment to denial, and mercy required that He delay it and precede it with clear warnings, He explained this and said: We destroyed them, and he had warned them before. Regarding His words ﴿Our assault﴾ there are two possibilities:

The first: what is meant is the assault that occurred, with which he had been threatening them, and this is indicated by His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾. It is as if He had said: We sent upon them what had been foretold; He mentioned it for the sake of warning and frightening them.

The second: what is meant by it is what is in the Hereafter, as in His words: ﴿On the Day when We will seize with the greatest seizing﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 16]. This is because all the messengers used to warn their peoples of the punishment of the Hereafter, as He said: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire blazing﴾, and He said: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Imminent﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and He said: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [an-Naba': 40] and so on, besides that. On this basis there is a subtle point: God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12], and here He said ﴿Our assault﴾ and did not say "We seized," because His words ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾ explain the genus of His seizing; so if its genus is severe, how much more so is the greatest of it. As for Lut, peace be upon him, he mentioned to them the greatest seizure, so that he would not be lax in conveying the message.
