Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they had sought to make him give up his guests, so We blotted out their eyes: "Taste My punishment and My warnings."﴾ *Al-murawadah* (seeking to persuade or entice someone) derives from *al-rawd* (seeking), and from it comes *al-iradah* (desire/will). It is close in meaning to *al-mutalabah* (demanding), except that *al-mutalabah* is used with the thing demanded directly, as when one says: Zayd demanded the dirhams from ʿAmr (*talaba Zaydun ʿAmran bi-l-darahim*). *Al-murawadah*, however, is used only with regard to an action, as when one says: he sought to persuade him to help (*rawadahu ʿan al-musaʿadah*). For this reason *al-murawadah* takes a second object with *ʿan* ("from"), while *al-mutalabah* takes it with *bi* ("with"). This is because the act depends on the choice of the agent, whereas the thing itself may come about without his choice. This is the difference in the situation. When you say, "Inform me of his matter" (*akhbirni bi-amrihi*), the information is specifically about the matter itself. This is unlike when one says "about such-and-such" (*ʿan kadha*). What makes this clearer is the speaker's saying, "Zayd informed me about the arrival of so-and-so" (*akhbarani Zayd ʿan majiʾ fulan*), and his saying, "He informed me of his arrival" (*akhbarani bi-majiʾihi*). For whoever says "about his arrival" (*ʿan majiʾihi*) may be informing about the manner of the arrival and not about the arrival itself, whereas "He informed me of his arrival" can only be about the arrival itself.

*Al-day︎f* (the guest) applies to one person and to a group. We have discussed this in the surah of al-Dhariyat. The manner of the seeking is mentioned earlier, namely that they were corrupters, and they heard of guests who had entered upon Lut, so they sought to persuade him to hand them over.

As for His saying ﴿so We blotted out their eyes﴾, we say: Jibril was among them, and he struck some of his wing over their faces, and so he blinded them.

There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first:** If the pronoun in *rawadahu* (they sought him) refers to the people of Lut, then the pronoun in *aʿyunahum* (their eyes) also refers to them, and so He would have blotted out the eyes of the people, when He blotted out only the eyes of a few of them, namely those who had entered Lut's house. If the pronoun refers to those who had entered the house, then there is no mention of them (in the verse), so how is this to be understood? We say: the seeking (*al-murawadah*) in reality was done by a group of them, but since the matter came from the people as a whole, and the others shared that view, it was attributed to all of them. Then by His saying *rawadahu* a group arose who were the actual seekers, and so the pronoun in *aʿyunihim* returns to them. An example of this is the speaker's saying: "Those who believed prayed, so their prayer was valid" (*alladhina amanu salla fa-sahhat salatuhum*). Here the pronoun in *salatihim* ("their prayer") refers to those who prayed after they believed, and does not refer merely to "those who believed". For if you limited yourself to "those who believed, so their prayer was valid", the speech would not be well-composed. But if you said, "Those who prayed, so their prayer was valid", the speech would be sound. Thus it is known that the pronoun returns to what arose after His saying *rawadahu*. And the pronoun in *rawadahu* refers to the warners who disputed the warnings (*al-mutamarina bi-l-nudhur*).

**The second issue:** He said here ﴿so We blotted out their eyes﴾, and in Yasin He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have blotted out their eyes﴾ [Yasin 36:66]. What is the difference? We say: This supports the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, for it is related from him that he said: The meaning of *al-tams* (blotting out) is the veiling from perception. Nothing was placed upon their sight, except that they entered and saw nothing there, so they were as though blinded. In Yasin, he meant that if He willed, He would have placed a covering upon their sight, that is, He would have stuck one of the two eyelids to the other, so that there would be a skin over the eye, and it would be as if it had been blotted out. Others said: they became blind, and their eyes became, together with their faces, like a single smooth surface. This is supported by His saying ﴿Taste My punishment﴾, because if they remained stubborn and saw nothing there, that would not be a punishment. And *al-tams* in the sense stated by others than Ibn ʿAbbas is a punishment. We say: The better view is that He, exalted is He, here relates what actually happened, namely the blotting out of the eye, the removal of its light and its form entirely, until their faces became like a smooth plate. They could not deny it, because it was an event that had occurred. As for the Yasin verse, He was warning them of something possible and within His power, so He chose what everyone would accept and recognize, namely blotting out over the eye, because the closing of the eyelid over the eye is a very common occurrence, and it is by the power and will of Allah, exalted is He. So He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have blotted out over their eyes﴾, and We did not split their eyelids open from their eyes. This is a matter of obvious possibility and very common occurrence. Whereas the blotting out that happened to the people of Lut was rare, so He said there, "over their eyes", so that it would be closer to acceptance.

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿Taste My punishment and My warnings﴾: to whom and with whom is this address made? We say there are several views:

**First:** There is an implied element; its sense is: "Then I said, through the tongues of the angels: Taste My punishment."

**Second:** This is an address to every denier; its sense is: "You used to deny, so taste My punishment," for when they denied, they tasted it.

**Third:** This speech follows the manner of human speech. When a king orders a criminal to be beaten, and he is extremely angry, and when he is beaten severely while crying out, and the king hears his cries, he says upon hearing his screams: "Taste it, for you are a criminal deserving of it." The king knows that the one being punished does not hear his words, and he addresses his words to the one who is seeking relief and crying out. This is common. Likewise, since everyone is in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, and is heard when He punishes an obstinate one with whom He is angry, He says: ﴿Taste it; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:49], ﴿So taste because you forgot the meeting of this your day﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:14], ﴿So taste My punishment﴾. He does not address one who hears and responds. This is the manifestation of justice, meaning: I am not unaware of your punishment, so that you might escape by crying out and supplication. Rather, I know about you, and you deserve this for what has proceeded from you. If it is said: this occurred without the *fa* (then), but with *fa* one does not say it, since with *fa* one may say: "You used to deny, so taste."

**The fourth issue:** How is *al-nudhur* (the warnings) tasted? We say: its meaning is: taste your action, that is, the requital of your action and its consequence. One says: "Taste the pain for your action" (*dhuq al-alam ʿala fiʿlika*). His saying ﴿So taste My punishment﴾ is like their saying, "Taste the pain," and His saying "and warnings" (*wa nudhur*) is like their saying, "Taste your action," that is, taste what followed from My warning. If it is said: according to this, the conjunction is not correct, because His saying ﴿So taste My punishment﴾ and "what followed from My warning, which is the punishment" would be like one saying: "Taste my punishment and my punishment?" We say: His saying ﴿So taste My punishment﴾ means the immediate part of it, and "what followed from My warning" means the deferred punishment, because the warning was made with it, as its explanation has preceded. So it is as though He said: "Taste My immediate punishment and My deferred punishment." If it is said: these two did not occur at the same time, so how can it be said "taste"? We say: the first part of the deferred punishment is connected to the last part of the immediate punishment, so they are like things occurring at one time. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh 71:25].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in the morning, a lasting punishment came upon them early.﴾ That is: the punishment which overtook the people after the particular one that blinded some of them. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿ṣabbahahum﴾ (came upon them in the morning) indicates the morning, so what is the meaning of "bukratan" (early)? We say its benefit is to specify the time of its onset within it. His saying "bukratan" may carry two aspects:

The first: that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). We say the same regarding His saying: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night (asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan)﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. There is a point of discussion here: al-Zamakhshari said, "What is the benefit of His saying 'laylan' (by night)?" One of them: "Or do you have, by virtue of your being a people, immunity?" So the one among you who persists does not fear, because he is among a people who have immunity.

The second: "Or do you have immunity if you persist?" Then the address is general and the threat is likewise general, and the condition is not mentioned, which is persistence.

**The second issue:** What is meant by His saying "better" (khayr)? The saying of a speaker "better" implies the sharing of two things in a praiseworthy quality with the preponderance of one over the other, and there was in them no good nor any praiseworthy quality? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

First: Denying that sharing is implied. This is shown by the saying of Ḥassān:

*You satirise him, but you are not his equal, so your evil is the ransom for your good.*

Along with the restriction of goodness to the Prophet, upon him be peace, and evil to the one who satirised him, and the absence of their sharing in anything of these.

Second: That this refers to what they claim, i.e., do your disbelievers claim that they are better than the earlier disbelievers who were destroyed? For they used to claim goodness for themselves. Likewise regarding those before them among the idol-worshippers and the deniers of the messengers, who used to say that the destruction occurred through heavenly causes, from the conjunction of the stars in a blameworthy configuration.

Third: What is meant is: are your disbelievers stronger? As if He said: "Are your disbelievers better in strength?" And strength is praiseworthy in common usage.

Fourth: Every existing thing is contingent, so in it are praiseworthy attributes and other, non-praiseworthy ones. When you look at the praiseworthy attributes in the two places and compare one with the other, you use for them the word "good" (khayr). Likewise, in blameworthy attributes the word "evil" (sharr) is used. So when you look at two disbelievers and say: "One of them is better than the other," then you may then mean: "One of them is better than the other in beauty and comeliness." And when you look at two believers who harm you, you say:

"One of them is worse than the other," meaning in harmfulness, not in faith. Likewise here: "Are your disbelievers better?" because the consideration fell on what would serve as a means of deliverance for them from punishment. It is like saying: "Do your disbelievers have something that delivers them, which was not in others, so that they are better, or is there nothing in them that delivers them, but God, by His grace, does not deliver them from it?"

**The third issue:** ﴿Or do you have immunity﴾ points to another cause of deliverance. For deliverance is either by means of something in them or it is not so. If it is by means of something in them, and that cause was not in those who preceded them, then they would be better than them. If it is not by means of something in them, then it is by the grace of God, His forgiveness toward them, and His granting them security from punishment. So He said to them: "Are you better than them, so that you will not perish? Or are you not better than them, but God has granted you security and destroyed them?" Each of these two is negated, so do not feel secure. As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Or do you have immunity in the Scriptures﴾, it points to a subtle point: that the intelligent person does not feel secure except when he has certainty of security, or there have come to him signs that bring the matter close to certainty. So He said: "Do you have an immunity that can be relied upon, repeated in the Books? For what is found in some Books may admit of interpretation, or distortion and alteration may have crept into it, as in the Torah and the Gospel." So He said: "Has there come to you a repeated immunity in Books by which you are secure from punishment? If it is not so, security is not permissible." But immunity is not found in any Book, nor in a single Book, nor in anything resembling a Book. So their security is from utmost heedlessness. At this point the excellence of the believer becomes clear, for even with what is in the Book of God, which falsehood does not approach from before it or behind it, of promise, he does not feel secure, even if he reaches the rank of the saints and the prophets, because of the possibility of specification in the verses of threat, and because each of them may be among those excepted from the community and cast out from it. So the believer is fearful and the disbeliever is secure in this world, and in the Hereafter the matter is the reverse.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united host, victorious"?﴾ This completes the explanation of the categories of deliverance (al-khalas) and confines it to them. The reason is that deliverance from punishment is either owed to the one delivered, as when a king punishes a group and among them is one who has done him a kindness, so he does not punish him; or it is due to some circumstance in the one delivered, as when he sees among them one who has a young child or a weak mother, so he has mercy on him even though he does not deserve it, and deliverance is written for him; or there is nothing in the one delivered that merits deliverance, nor anything in the punisher himself that calls for mercy, but he is unable to act against him because of the multitude of his helpers and the partisanship of his brothers. This is like when a man flees from the king and takes refuge with an army that prevents the king from reaching him. Thus, just as He negated the first two categories, He also negated the third, which is protection through helpers and the factionalism of kinsmen. There are several issues here:

The first issue: on the excellence of the ordering. The one who deserves punishment in himself is closer to deliverance than the one who is shown mercy, for the one who deserves it does not have the cause of punishment present in him, whereas the one shown mercy has that cause present in him, and there is also an obstacle to the punishment. What has no cause does not come into being at all, while what has an obstacle may not be such that the obstacle is strong enough to repel the cause. The obstacle that lies within the punisher himself is stronger than that which comes from another, because the one that comes from within him prevents the motive, and the act does not come about when the motive is absent. The one that comes from another, through protection, does not cut off his intention; rather he strives, and perhaps prevails, so that his punishment becomes many times what it was before. This is unlike one whose heart is softened and whom mercy restrains; though mercy does not prevent him entirely, it does not increase his burden, his imprisonment, or his additional punishment when he has the power. This is an arrangement of the utmost excellence.

The second issue: (jami') has two benefits. One is multitude, and the other is agreement, as if he had said: "We are many and united, so victory is ours." No other single word can take its place among simple terms. We say it has two benefits because the word jam' indicates a group by its original letters j-m-' and by its pattern, fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning that they have gathered their collective fanaticism (ʿaṣabiyya). The third issue: why is "al-muntasir" singular, when "nahnu" is a plural pronoun? We say: on the first interpretation it is clear, because it describes the other component that occurs as the predicate. It is like the saying of one who says: "You are a victorious kind, and they are a dominant host." The word jami' is like jins (kind): its form is singular, but its meaning is plural, containing multitude. As for the second interpretation, the answer to it is in two ways:

The first: although the meaning is "all of the people, with nothing outside them except whoever is not counted," yet when it is made definite by the idafa being cut and given tanwin, it becomes like an indefinite noun in origin, so it is permissible to describe it with an indefinite term, looking to the wording; thus it returns to the first interpretation.

The second: that it is a predicate following a predicate, and it is permissible for one of the two predicates to be definite and the other indefinite. God said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving﴾ ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ ﴿Doer of what He intends﴾ [al-Buruj: 14–16]. On this basis, His saying ﴿We are a united host, victorious﴾ uses the singular because it is adjacent to "jami'." It may also be said that the meaning of ﴿We are a united host, victorious﴾ is that jami' means "each one," as if He had said: "Each one of us is victorious," just as you say: "They are all strong," meaning each one of them is strong, or "They are all scholars," meaning each one is a scholar. So He left the plural and chose the singular because the predicate refers back to each individual. They used to say: "Each one of us will overcome Muhammad ﷺ," as Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi said. This contains a subtle meaning: they claimed that each one of them was victorious, and God refuted them all together with His saying:

﴿The multitude will be routed, and they will turn their backs.﴾ The meaning is that they claimed a general strength by which each one of them would overcome Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah, exalted is He, showed their manifest weakness, which encompasses them all, by His saying: ﴿and they will turn their backs.﴾ At this point a question arises: He said ﴿ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ (*wa-yuwallūna al-dubura*, "and they will turn the back") and did not say *yuwallūna al-adbār* (the plural form). In another place He said: ﴿They will not harm you except for a little injury; and if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111]. He also said: ﴿And they had already promised Allah before that they would not turn their backs﴾ [al-Ahzab: 15], and in another place: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve [in battle], do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15]. So how is the singular form to be justified, and what is the difference between these passages?

We say: As for the justification, it is evident, because the saying of the speaker "they did" is like his saying "he did this, and he did that, and the other did," (where the plural refers to each individually). They said: the *wāw al-jamʿ* (the plural *wāw*, the "wāw of plurality") takes the place of the *wāws* that occur in coordination (*ʿaṭf*). And His saying ﴿يُوَلُّونَ﴾ (*yuwallūna*, "they turn") is equivalent to: this one turns his back, and that one turns, and the other one turns; that is, each one turns his own back.

As for the difference, we say: the context of the final verses requires the singular form as the more appropriate. So His saying ﴿ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ with the singular indicates that they, in turning away, were like a single soul, so none of them lags behind the group, and none of them stands firm against the onslaught. They were, in turning away, like one back. We say: the appointed time (mawʿid) is the time in which the promise and the threat occur. The believer is promised good and commanded to be patient, so he does not say, "When will it be?" Rather, he entrusts the matter to God. As for the disbeliever, he does not affirm it, so he says, "When will the punishment be?" It is said to him: "Be patient, for it is coming on the Day of Resurrection." The second issue: More calamitous than what? We say: it admits of two meanings:

One of them: the kinds of punishment of this world that have passed.

The second: "more calamitous of calamities," so there is no calamity like it.

The third issue: What is meant by His saying: ﴿and more bitter﴾? We say: there are two views on it:

One of them: it is an intensive form of "bitter" (murr), and it is suitable to His saying: ﴿So taste My punishment﴾ and His saying: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾. On this view, "more calamitous" means more severe, and "more bitter" means more painful. The difference between the severe (shadid) and the painful (alim) is that "severe" indicates that no one can bear it because of its intensity, and no one can repel it by his own strength. An example: a weak person thrown into water that overcomes him, or into a fire from which he cannot escape; and a strong person thrown into a vast sea or a great fire — both are equal in pain and torment, and equal in causing suffering, but they differ in severity. The rescue of the weak person from the weak water is possible with the help of a helper, while the rescue of the strong person from the great sea is not possible.

The second: "more bitter" is an intensive form of "passing by" (al-marr), for it passes over them more often, indicating permanence. It is as if He says: more severe and more lasting. This applies specifically to the punishment of the Hereafter, for if the punishment of this world becomes severe, the one punished is killed and it ends, so it does not last; and if it lasts such that one is not killed, then it is not severe.

The third: that it means "bitter" (marir), which is from "strength" (mirrah), meaning severity. On this view, either the statement is like the speaker's saying: "So-and-so is lean and emaciated, and strong and severe," bringing two synonymous words to indicate emphasis — and this is weak; or "more calamitous" is an intensive form of "calamity" (dahiyah), the active participle of "dahahu amru kadha" when a matter befalls him, and this is a difficult matter, because "calamity" has become like a noun assigned to the severe, on the pattern of "al-bateyah" and "al-sa'ibah," which are not among the active participles, although the origin of "dahiyah" is that. It has been used as a noun and written in its chapters. On this view its meaning is more binding and more constricting, i.e., it is of such a kind that it cannot be repelled.

First: For whom was the verse revealed? Most of the exegetes agree that it was revealed concerning the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya). Al-Wahidi narrated in his Tafsir, saying: I heard Shaykh Radi al-Din al-Mu'ayyad al-Tusi in Nishapur say: I heard Abd al-Jabbar say: Al-Wahidi informed us, saying: Abu al-Qasim Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Sarraj informed us, saying: Abu Muhammad Abd Allah al-Ka'bi informed us, saying: Hamdan ibn Salih al-Ashajj narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Dawud narrated to us: Sufyan al-Thawri narrated to us, from Ziyad ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi, from Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Ja'far, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The polytheists of Quraysh came disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about predestination (qadar), so God Most High revealed: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]." Likewise it is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that this verse was revealed concerning the Qadariyya.

It is also narrated from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The Magians of this community are the Qadariyya." And they are the criminals whom God Most High named in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾. The traditions concerning the Qadariyya are numerous, and there are discussions concerning them:

The first: concerning the meaning of the Qadariyya about whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said that the verse was revealed. We say: each group, in the matter of the creation of actions, holds that the Qadari is its opponent. The Jabriyya (determinists) say: the Qadari is one who says that obedience and disobedience are not created by God, nor by His decree and predestination; so they are Qadariyya because they deny predestination. The Mu'tazili says: the Qadari is the Jabri who says, when he commits adultery and steals, "God has decreed it for me," so he is a Qadari because of his affirmation of predestination. Both of them say to the People of the Sunna: the one who acknowledges God's creation and that nothing is from the servant is a Qadari. The truth is that the Qadari about whom the verse was revealed is the one who denies predestination and says that all events occur by the stars and their conjunctions. This is indicated by his saying: "The polytheists of Quraysh came disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about predestination," for their doctrine was that, and they did not say what the Mu'tazila say: "God created for me soundness of limbs and power of perception, and enabled me to obey and disobey, and God is able to compel obedience and compel disobedience, and able to feed the poor whom I feed by God's grace." The polytheists used to say: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if God willed, He would feed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47], denying God's power to provide food. As for his saying (ﷺ): "The Magians of this community are the Qadariyya," we say: the intended "this community" is either the community to which Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, whether they believed in him or not, as in the phrase "the people," or his community who believed in him. If the first is meant, then the Qadariyya in his time were the polytheists who denied God's power over events, and so the Mu'tazila do not enter among them. If the second is meant, then his saying "the Magians of this community" means those whose relation to this community is like the relation of the Magians to earlier communities; but most of the earlier communities were unbelievers, and the Magians were a kind of them with weaker proof and greater opposition to reason. Likewise the Qadariyya in this community are a kind of them with weaker proof, and this does not entail a certainty that they are in the Fire. The truth is that the Qadari is the one who denies God's power, if we say the relation is to negation, or the one who affirms the power of other than God over events, if we say the relation is to affirmation; and then it is certain that he is ﴿in error and madness﴾ and that he tastes the touch of Saqar.

The second discussion: concerning who among those professing to be from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) enters the Qadariyya mentioned in the text. If we say the Qadariyya were so named for their denial of God's power, then one who says that God has no power to move the servant with a movement that is prayer and a movement that is fornication, although that is possible, is not far from being included among them. As for one who says that God is able, but did not compel him and left him with the servant's own motivation, like a father who tests a child in carrying something, leaving him to it not from the father's incapacity but for trial and examination, not like the paralytic who has no strength when he says to another: carry this—such a one does not enter among them outwardly, even if he is mistaken. If we say the Qadariyya were so named for affirming the power over events for other than God, from the stars, then:

As for his saying (ﷺ): "The Magians of this community are the Qadariyya," we say: the intended "this community" is either the community to which Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, whether they believed in him or not, as in the phrase "the people," or his community who believed in him. If the first is meant, then the Qadariyya in his time were the polytheists who denied God's power over events, and so the Mu'tazila do not enter among them. If the second is meant, then his saying "the Magians of this community" means those whose relation to this community is like the relation of the Magians to earlier communities; but most of the earlier communities were unbelievers, and the Magians were a kind of them with weaker proof and greater opposition to reason. Likewise the Qadariyya in this community are a kind of them with weaker proof, and this does not entail a certainty that they are in the Fire. The truth is that the Qadari is the one who denies God's power, if we say the relation is to negation, or the one who affirms the power of other than God over events, if we say the relation is to affirmation; and then it is certain that he is ﴿in error and madness﴾ and that he tastes the touch of Saqar.

The second discussion: concerning who among those professing to be from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) enters the Qadariyya mentioned in the text. If we say the Qadariyya were so named for their denial of God's power, then one who says that God has no power to move the servant with a movement that is prayer and a movement that is fornication, although that is possible, is not far from being included among them. As for one who says that God is able, but did not compel him and left him with the servant's own motivation, like a father who tests a child in carrying something, leaving him to it not from the father's incapacity but for trial and examination, not like the paralytic who has no strength when he says to another: carry this—such a one does not enter among them outwardly, even if he is mistaken. If we say the Qadariyya were so named for affirming the power over events for other than God, from the stars, then:

[Page 63]
and the Jabri who said: he is the fallen wall for which it is not permissible to impose obligation on anything, because the act proceeds from another; these are the people of permissiveness (ibaha). There is no doubt that he enters the Qadariyya, for he disbelieves by denying obligation. As for one who says: God Most High created actions in us and decreed them and obligated us, and ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]—he is not among them.

The third discussion: The disputants differed in partisanship as to whether the name is more fitting for the Mu'tazila or for the Ash'ariyya. The Mu'tazila said: the name is more fitting for you, because the attribution is to affirmation, not to negation. It is said of the materialist (dahri) "dahri" because of his saying of time (dahr) and affirming it; of the libertine "ibahi" because of his affirming permissiveness; of the Dualists "thanawi" because of their affirming the two, namely light and darkness; and similarly its examples. And you affirm predestination. The Ash'ariyya said: the texts indicate that the Qadari is the one who negates God's power, and the polytheists of Quraysh were Qadariyya only because they affirmed a power for other than God. The Mu'tazila said: the polytheists were named Qadariyya only because they said: if He is able over events, as you say, O Muhammad, then if God willed He would guide us, and if He willed He would feed the poor; so they believed that among the necessary consequences of God's power over events is His creating guidance in them if He wills. This is your doctrine, O Ash'ariyya. The plain truth is that each of the Muslims who went to either of the two doctrines is outside the Qadariyya, and none of them becomes a Qadari unless the negator becomes a negator of power and the affirmer becomes a denier of obligation.

The second issue: The criminals here are the polytheists, as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when the criminals hang their heads﴾ [al-Sajda: 12], and His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and His saying: ﴿The criminals are known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. The verse is general, even if it was revealed concerning a particular people. Their crime is denying the messengers and warners by associating partners with God, denying the Gathering, and denying God's power to revive after death, and over other events.

The third issue: ﴿in error and madness﴾ admits of three aspects:

One: the combination of the two matters in this world, that is: they are in this world in error and madness, not understanding and not guided. On this view, His saying ﴿the Day they are dragged﴾ explains their state in that situation, and this is closer.

Second: the combination in the Hereafter, that is: they are in the error of the Hereafter and in madness too. As for madness, their being in it is clear; as for error, they do not find their way to their goal or to anything suitable as a goal, while they are bewildered as to the way. If it is said: the correct view is the last alone, because His saying ﴿the Day they are dragged﴾ is the adverbial object of the speech, that is: on the Day they are dragged, it will be said to them, "Taste"—and we will explain this—we say: ﴿the Day they are dragged﴾ may be governed by an expressed verb or an understood unexpressed verb. The first possibility has two aspects:

One: the governing verb is prior, and it is a meaning that is existent and fixed, except that this has become forgotten.

Second: the governing verb is later, and it is His saying ﴿Taste﴾; its estimated form is: "Taste the touch of Saqar on the Day the criminals are dragged," and the address then is with those addressed in His saying ﴿Are your unbelievers better than those, or do you have immunity?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43].

The third possibility: the understood element is that it is said to them, "On the Day they are dragged, taste," and this is the well-known view. His saying ﴿Taste﴾ is a metaphor, and in it is wisdom: taste is among the perceptions, for what is tasted, when it touches the tongue, also perceives its heat, coldness, roughness and smoothness, as the rest of the sensory organs perceive; it also perceives its flavor, which no organ other than the tongue perceives. So the perception of the tongue is more complete. When one is harmed by fire, he is harmed by its heat and its bitterness, whereas if it is hot, others are harmed only by its heat. Thus taste is a tactile perception more complete than others among things touched. So He said ﴿Taste﴾, indicating that their perception through taste is the most complete of perceptions, so that intensity of punishment combines with its pain through its long duration and perpetuity, and the one who perceives it has no excuse that could occupy him, but is at the most complete state of perception, so that great pain results. We have mentioned that according to the view of most, one says to them, or we say, with an implied verb. We have also mentioned that there is no need for an implied verb if the address is with someone other than those about whom it was said, ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error﴾; for it becomes as if He said: "Taste, you who deny Muhammad (ﷺ), the touch of Saqar on the Day the criminals who preceded into the Fire are dragged."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾, and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: It is well known that His saying ﴿Indeed, everything﴾ is connected to what precedes it, as if He said: "Taste! Indeed, We have created everything in measure," meaning that this is a recompense for those who denied it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. The apparent meaning, however, is that it is the beginning of a new statement, and the speech was complete at His saying: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾. Then He mentioned the description of the punishment, because the conjunction in ﴿And Our command is but one﴾ [al-Qamar: 50] indicates that His saying ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾ is not the last of the speech. This is also indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾, and He had already mentioned creation in the first verse with His saying ﴿Indeed, We have created everything﴾, so it is fitting that He should mention command, and so He said: ﴿And Our command is but one﴾. As for what was mentioned of the disputation, we say: The Prophet (ﷺ) held them to account with His saying ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error﴾ up to His saying ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾, and he recited another verse with the intention of recitation, and he did not recite the final verse, being content with the knowledge of the one who knows the verse, just as you say in proofs: ﴿Do not consume your wealth﴾ [al-Nisa: 29], the verse, and ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121], the verse, and ﴿When you contract a debt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], the verse, and so on.

The second issue: ﴿Kulla﴾ (every) is read in the accusative, which is the more correct and well-known reading, and in the nominative. Whoever reads it in the accusative, its accusative is due to a hidden verb which the apparent one explains, as in His saying: ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39], and His saying: ﴿And for the wrongdoers He has prepared for them﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. That verb is "khalaqnahu" (We created it), and His saying "khalaqnahu" explains it, as if He said: "Indeed, We created everything in measure." "Khalaqnahu" in this construction cannot be an attribute of a thing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And of every thing We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49]. However, there, what prevents it from being an attribute is that it is devoid of a pronoun referring back to the described noun, and here this preventing factor is not present. On this basis, the verse is a proof against the Mu'tazilah, because our actions are a "thing," so they fall within "every thing," and therefore they are created by God, exalted is He. Whoever reads it in the nominative cannot say what he says in His saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17], where it is read in the nominative, because "kulla shay'" is indefinite, so it is not valid as a subject, and it would follow that he must say: "Every thing We created, it is in measure," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned these two aspects in his tafsir, and he mentioned that the Mu'tazili holds on to the reading in the nominative. It is possible to say that the first reading, the accusative, has another aspect, which is that its accusative is due to a known verb, not a hidden explained one, namely "qaddarna" or "khalaqna," as if He said: "Indeed, We created everything—We created it in measure," or "We determined everything—We created it in measure." We only said that it is known because His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of everything﴾ [Ghafir: 62] indicates it, and His saying ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾ indicates that it is a measure. In that case, there is no indication in the verse against the Mu'tazili's view; it only refutes the statement ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾. As for the second reading, the nominative, we say: It is permissible that "kull shay'" be the subject and "khalaqnahu bi-qadar" its predicate, and in that case the proof is established against them in the most forceful manner.

And His saying ﴿kull shay'﴾ is indefinite, so it is not suitable as a subject, is weak, because His saying "kull shay'" encompasses all things entirely, so there is not in it the objection that applies to our saying "a man is standing," since that does not convey any clear benefit. And His saying ﴿kull shay'﴾ conveys what "Zayd, We created him" and "'Amr, We created him" convey, with an added benefit. For this reason they permitted "mā aḥadun khayrun minka" (no one is better than you), because it conveys generality, whereas the saying of one who says "aḥadun khayrun minka" (someone is better than you) is not good, since it does not convey generality.

The third issue: What is the meaning of qadar (measure)? We say: There are several aspects to it:

The first: It is quantity, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾. On this basis, everything is measured in its essence and in its attributes. As for what is measured in essence, it is the body, and this is evident in it; likewise, what subsists in the body among sensible things, such as whiteness and blackness. As for the indivisible atom, it has no quantity, and what subsists in the atom has no quantity in the sense of extension, such as knowledge, ignorance, and others. We say: here there are quantities that are not in the sense of extension. As for the indivisible atom, two of them are smaller than three, and were it not that a volume increases extension by it, it would not have occurred without extension in it. As for what subsists in the atom, it has a limit and a beginning, so the quantity of the created knowledges and the created powers is finite. As for the attribute, that is because everything that has a beginning in time has a quantity in its duration, since everything is originated. If it is said: God, exalted is He, is described by it, and He has no quantity and no beginning to His existence, we say: When a speaker is described by an attribute or named by a name, then mentions things named by that name or described by that attribute, and attributes to them an action of his from which he is excluded, as one says: "I saw all who are in this house, and they all honored me," and says: "There is no one in the house but who struck me or whom I struck," he is excluded from it, not because he is not the subject of the name, but by what the construction contains of evidence for his exclusion from the will. Likewise His saying ﴿We created it﴾ and ﴿the Creator of everything﴾ excludes Him from it, not by way of specification but by way of reality, if we say that the construction is conventional, for this construction was then not established except for other than the speaker.

The second: qadar is determination. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We determined, and excellent are the determiners﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23], and the poet said:

"And the Merciful has determined what He is able to do"

meaning: He determined what is determined. On this basis, the meaning is that God, exalted is He, did not create anything without determination, as an archer shoots an arrow and it lands in a place he had not determined; rather God created as He determined. This is unlike the view of the philosophers that He is an agent by His essence and that difference is due to the receptacles: whatever comes short or small is due to the readiness of its matter, and whatever comes long or large is due to another readiness. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Everything We created in measure﴾ from Us. Thus the small may be large, and the large may be created small.

The third: ﴿bi-qadar﴾ is what is said together with qada' (decree). It is said: "by the decree of God and His qadar." The philosophers, regarding the qadar that accompanies qada', said: what is intended is qada', and what necessarily follows is qadar. Thus they say: the creation of fire as hot is by decree, and it is decreed because it ought to be so; but among its necessary consequences is that if it touches the cotton of an old woman or falls upon the reeds of a pauper, it burns it, and this is by qadar, not by qada'. This is corrupt speech. Rather, qada' is what is in knowledge and qadar is what is in will. So His saying ﴿Everything We created in measure﴾ means: in measure with His will, not as they claim, that it is necessitated—a refutation of the polytheists.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾

That is, it is but one word, namely His saying to it: "Be" (kun) [Yasin 36:82]. This is the well-known and apparent meaning. On this view, when God wills something, He says to it "Be," so there are two things: the will (irada) and the speech (qawl). The will is qadar (divine measure), and the speech is qada' (divine decree). His saying "one" (wahida) may carry two meanings. The first is to show that there is no need to repeat the word, indicating the immediate effect of the command. The second is to show that His state does not vary: His command at the creation of the mighty Throne is like His command at the creation of the tiny ant, so His command is one in every case. His saying "like a glance of the eye" is a comparison of the occurrence (kawn), not a comparison of the command. It is as if He said: "Our command is one, so the thing commanded comes into being like a glance of the eye," because if it referred to the command itself, that would not be a fitting description of praise, since the word "Be" is also a thing that comes into existence ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾.

This is the apparent and well-known explanation. There is also a clear view taken by the philosophers (hukama'): that the objects of God's power are the possible things (mumkinat), which He brings into existence by His power. There is disagreement about their non-existence, but its explanation is not fitting for this place because of its length, and for no other reason. Next, the possible things that God brings into existence are of two kinds.

The first kind consists of things that have parts which, when they come together, complete their existence, such as humans, animals, plants, and minerals. Likewise the four elements, the heavens, all other bodies, and all accidents that subsist in bodies. All of these are both measured for Him and created in time, since their parts come into existence first, and then composition and combination come into being in them. So in them there are measures, considered in terms of their parts, their composition, and their accidents.

The second kind consists of things that have no parts, joints, or extended magnitudes: the noble spirits that give light to bodies. All the philosophers affirmed these except a few, and a group of the theologians (mutakallimun) agreed with them. Many who have a heart among the people of spiritual exercises (riyadat) and the people of striving (mujahadat) have asserted them with certainty. The existence of these things is one; they do not come into existence first as parts and then have those parts assembled, unlike bodies and the accidents that subsist in them.

Once you know this, they say: bodies are created by measure (khalqiyya qadariyya), and spirits are originated by command (ibda'iyya amriyya). They say that God's words point to this: ﴿Surely, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 7:54]. So creation (khalq) belongs to bodies, and command (amr) belongs to spirits.

They then say: one should not suppose that this statement contradicts the reports. For the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first thing God created was the intellect." It is also narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "God created the spirits two thousand years before the bodies." God also said: ﴿God is the Creator of everything﴾. So creation (khalq) is applied to the bringing into existence of spirits and the intellect, because applying the term "creation" to what is also described as "command" is permissible. And since the whole world is originated, applying "creation" in the sense of "bringing into being" (ihdath) is permissible, even though in the strict linguistic sense creation (khalq) involves measuring. The sense of "bringing into being" does not involve that. Were it not for the difference between these two expressions, the philosopher would find it as objectionable to say "the created is eternal" as he finds it objectionable to say "the originated is eternal."

The Prophet's (ﷺ) words "God created the spirits" mean "He brought them into being by His command." In this usage there is a great benefit: if he (ﷺ) had changed the expression and said that spirits exist by command while bodies exist by creation, the one whom God has not granted much knowledge would have thought that the spirit is not created, in the sense of not originated. He would then have gone astray. The Prophet (ﷺ) was sent as a mercy.

They also say: when you consider God's words ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra' 17:85], and His words ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf 7:54], and His words ﴿Then We made the drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump, then We made the lump into bones﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:14], you find a difference between command and creation, and between spirits and bodily forms. He assigned to the creation of some bodies a long period of time, namely six days, and He assigned to others a sequence and succession by His words ﴿Then We made﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:14] and ﴿So We made﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:14]. He did not assign such a thing to the spirit.

They then say: one should not suppose from what we have said that bodies necessarily require a long period of time and days in which God brings them into being. Rather, God is free to choose: if He wills to create the heavens, the earth, humans, animals, trees, and plants in less than the blink of an eye, He would create them so. But even so, they do not cease to be existents that have parts, and the existence of their parts before the existence of composition in them, and their existence after the existence of parts and composition in them. So they are six, three times three, just as God creates breaking and being broken in a single time, yet there is a rational order between them. Thus a body, however you suppose its creation, contains in it measured existences, all brought into being by God in order. The spirit has a single existence brought into being by God, exalted is He. This is their view.

Let us now mention the aspects of creation and command, both transmitted and rational:

The first: what we mentioned, that command is the word "Be," and creation is what is by power and will.

The second: what they mentioned about bodies, that among them are spirits.

The third: God has a power by which He brings into being, and a will by which He specifies. This is because the originated thing has an existence specific to a time and a determined measure. Its existence is by power, and its specification to a time is by will. So what is by His power is creation, and what is by will is command, since He specifies it to a time by His command. This is indicated by both transmitted and rational evidence. As for the transmitted evidence, it is His words ﴿When He wills a thing, He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:82]. He made "Be" tied to the connection of will. Know that what is meant by "Be" is not the letters and word made of kaf and nun, because occurrence is faster than the word "Be" if you take it in its literal sense. The letters kaf and nun cannot come from one speaker except in sequence. So in "Be" there is a word of time, and the being (kawn) comes after it, as shown by His words ﴿and it is﴾ with the particle "fa" (then). So if "Be" meant the literal letter and sound, the occurrence would come after it in time, and this is not the case. If someone says: it is possible for the two letters to exist together, and God's speech is not like our speech, which requires time, we reply: He has given it a meaning other than what we understand from the wording.

As for the rational evidence: specification to a time has no cause or purpose. Although some people have held that creation and bringing into being are for a wisdom, and say that God created the earth to be a dwelling place for people, or something similar of this sort of wisdom, they cannot say: He created the earth at that specific time so that it would be a dwelling for them, because if He had created it at another time, it would still have been a dwelling for them. Therefore, the specification has no reason; it is pure wisdom. It resembles the command of a mighty king, who commands and is not asked, "Why did you command this, and why did you do that?" The intention of the one who commands is known only from him.

The fourth: created things do not escape three attributes, or two opposite attributes. For example, a body, after its creation, must be in a space, and it must be either at rest or in motion. So its bringing into being first by creation, and what it is in by command, is indicated by His words ﴿Surely your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ up to His words ﴿subjected by His command﴾ [al-A'raf 7:54]. He made what belongs to them after their creation, of motion, rest, and other things, to be by His command. This is also indicated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "The first thing God Most High created was the intellect. He said to it: 'Come forward,' and it came forward. Then He said to it: 'Turn back,' and it turned back." Here he made creation to be in essence and command to be in attribute. Likewise His words ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾, then He said ﴿He manages the command from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾. We have already explained this.

The fifth: God's created things are of two kinds. The first: what God created in the quickest possible way, like the intellect and others. The second: what He created with a period of waiting, like the heavens, humans, animals, and plants. The thing created quickly was described as command, and the thing created with a period of waiting was described as creation. This is similar to the second aspect.

The sixth: what Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said in interpreting His words ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ [Fussilat 41:11]. It is that creation is measuring and bringing into being, and what follows it is a sequence of order, not a sequence of time. So in God's knowledge it is that the heavens will become seven heavens in two days, as a measure. He measured their creation as He knew it, and this is bringing into being. Thus the first (measuring) is creation, and the second, which is bringing into being, is command. This is taken from the linguistic meaning. A poet said:

"And some people measure, then do not cut."

That is, he measures but does not cut or separate, like the tailor who first measures and then cuts. This is close to the lexical meaning, but it is far from usage in the Qur'an, because wherever God mentions creation He means bringing into being. From this is His words ﴿And if you asked them who created them﴾ [Luqman 31:25], and from it His words ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:77]. It is not meant that We measured that something would come into being from it, or anything else of that sort.

The seventh: creation is bringing into being from the beginning, and command is that by which restoration occurs. God created the creatures first over a period of time, and then on the Day of Resurrection He will raise them in less than a moment. So His words ﴿And Our command is but one﴾ are like His words ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ [al-Saffat 37:19], and ﴿a single cry﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:29], and ﴿a single blast﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:13]. On this view, His words ﴿Surely We created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar 54:49] point to unity. His words ﴿And Our command is but one﴾ extend to the Gathering, so it is as if He explained the first origin and the last origin through the verses.

The eighth: bringing into being is creation, and annihilation is command. That is, He says to the stern, severe angels: "Destroy" and "Act," and they do not disobey God in what He commands them, nor do they delay compliance until the command is repeated a second time. So His command once brings annihilation and destruction in its wake.

Among its subtleties: God Most High placed the bringing-into-existence, which belongs to mercy, in His own hand, while destruction He entrusts to His messengers and angels. He placed death in the hand of the Angel of Death, but He did not place life in the hand of any angel. This fits this context, because He explained the blessing with His words, "Indeed, all things We have created with measure" [54:49], and He explained His power over retribution, so He said, "And Our command is but one" [54:50], and "And indeed, We are able to take it away" [23:18]. This is like His saying, "So when Our command came and the oven boiled over" [11:40], at the time of punishment; and His saying, "So when Our command came, We saved Salih" [11:66]; and His saying, "So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest" [11:82]. Just as He mentioned the punishment in these narratives with the word "command," and explained the destruction with it, so too here. This is especially so if you consider the narratives that preceded and find them the very same narratives, which strengthens this view. Likewise His saying, "And We have already destroyed your like, so is there any who will remember?" [54:51] indicates the correctness of this view.

Ninth: Regarding the meaning of "like the blink of an eye" (al-lamh bil-basar), there are two views. The first: it is looking with the eye, as one says "I glanced at him with my sight," just as one says "I looked at him with my eye," and the bi- here is like that mentioned in verses, as one says "I wrote with the pen." He chose this example because looking with the eye is the swiftest movement found in a human being, since the eye contains features that help speed of movement. The first: its closeness to the mover, for the mover is the nervous system, whose origin is the brain, and the eye is extremely close to it. The second: the smallness of its size, for it does not resist the mover and is not heavy upon it, unlike bones. The third: the roundness of its shape, for rolling a sphere is easier than rolling a square or a triangle. The fourth: its being in a moist substance created in the organ that is its place. This is the wisdom behind the fact that visible things are extremely numerous, unlike eaten things, heard things, objects reached by the feet, and tasted things. Were it not for the swiftness of the movement of the instrument by which visible things are perceived, it would not reach the whole except after a long time.

The second: "the glancing with the sight" means lightning that snatches at the sight and passes by it swiftly, and the bi- here is for adhesion (ilsaq), not for instrumentality, as in saying "I passed by him" (marartu bihi), and that is in the utmost speed. His saying "with the sight" carries a benefit, namely the utmost speed; for if He had said "like the flash of lightning when it flashes," which begins its movement from one place and ends at another place in the least time that can be imagined, it would still be correct. Yet, even so, the amount that passes through the sight is less than what occurs from its starting point to its endpoint. So He said "like a glance" (kalamh), not as is said, "from the beginning to the end," but rather the amount that passes through the sight, which is the utmost paucity and the extreme of swiftness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verse 51–53:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly destroyed your like-minded predecessors, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Al-ashya' (الأشياع) means the likes, the similar ones. And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 9–11]. And: ﴿fa'aluhu (فَعَلُوهُ)﴾ is an attribute of "shay'" (thing), and an indefinite noun may be described by clauses.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And every small and great [matter] is recorded (mustatar)﴾ is a generalization of the ruling, meaning that writing is not limited to what they did; rather, what others did as well is [recorded]. It is inscribed, so nothing goes out of the books, neither small nor great. We have already mentioned, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth escapes Him, nor is there anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear register﴾ [Saba': 3], that in the saying ﴿greater (akbar)﴾ there is a great benefit, namely that whoever writes down a person's account does so, in most cases, so that he does not forget. So when [a matter] is grand and one feels safe from forgetting it, he may leave off writing it and occupy himself with writing what he fears forgetting. Therefore, when He said: ﴿nor greater﴾ from that, He indicated that the great matters, of which one is secure from forgetting, are [nonetheless] written down; that is, Our recording is not like your recording, whose purpose is security from forgetting. So we say here, and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is with this Book that leaves neither small nor great [matter] but that it has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and in all these places He placed "small" first, because it is more suitable for precision in writing, so one begins with it, as a safeguard against forgetting, in the customary practice of people. Thus God has ordered the mention [of these matters] according to their customs. This supports what we mentioned earlier, that "kull" (كُلّ), although indefinite in form, is good to begin with for generality and to avoid ambiguity.

**Verse 54:** Then He, the Exalted, said:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and a river.﴾ We have already explained the meaning of "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqun) and "the gardens" in several surahs, among them ﴿by the Mount (al-Tur)﴾. As for "river" (nahar), there are recitations (qira'at) of it, among them the reading with a fatha on the nun and the ha, like hajar (rock). It is an ism jins (generic noun) and stands in place of "rivers." This is the apparent and most correct reading. On it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** There is no doubt that the complete pleasure of a garden lies in a person being within it, and that the pleasure of a river does not lie in a person being in it. Rather, his pleasure is to be in Paradise beside the river. So what is the meaning of His saying ﴿and a river﴾? We say: We have already answered this in the explanation of His saying ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ in Surat al-Dhariyat, where we said that what is meant is "among the springs," and the space between them. Likewise with "in gardens," because the garden is the trees that shade the rays of the sun. For this reason He said ﴿in shades and springs﴾ [al-Mursalat: 41]. And if the garden is the shading trees, then a person is not in the trees; rather he is among them or between them. Likewise with the river. We will add here another aspect: what is meant is "in gardens and beside a river," because proximity makes acceptable the use of a word that would not be acceptable in the absence of proximity, as the poet said:

*"I fed her straw and cold water."*

And they said: "I girded myself with a sword and a spear," but water is not fed, and a spear is not girded. Yet because of the proximity of straw to water and of the sword to the spear, the expression is acceptable. Likewise here, He did not use in the second case what He used in the first, the word *fi* ("in").

**Page 70**

**The second issue:** He used the singular "river" with the plural "gardens," and in many places He used the plural "rivers," as in His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ and other places. What is the wisdom in this? We say: As for the first answer, when He explained that the meaning of *fi nahar* ("in a river") is "among," the listener had no need to hear "rivers," since he knows that a single river does not have "among" it. As for His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, had He not used the plural "rivers," one might have understood that in all the gardens there is one river, as in this world. Rather, a single river may extend and flow through many gardens. As for the second answer, we say: A person is in gardens, because we have made clear that the plural "gardens" indicates their vastness, the abundance and variety of their trees. The singular was used when He said ﴿the likeness of Paradise﴾ [Muhammad: 15] and said ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for [the price of] that the Garden will be theirs﴾ [al-Tawba: 111], because its trees are interconnected and no barren stretches of land fall between them. Once you know this, a person in this world, if he is in a house, and that house is in a neighbourhood, and that neighbourhood is in a city, it is said that he is in such-and-such a town. As for proximity: if a person in this world is between two rivers such that his nearness to them is equal, it is said that he is sitting beside two rivers. If he comes nearer to one of them, it is said that he is beside one of the two rivers and not the other. But in the abode of this world it is not possible for a person to be beside three rivers; he can only be beside two, and a third is farther than the two. So in reality he is not, at one time, beside three rivers. And God, the Exalted, speaks of the matter of the Hereafter in terms of what we understand in this world, so He said "beside a river," because we have made clear that His saying ﴿and a river﴾, although it implies "in a river," that is due to proximity, as in "I girded myself with a sword and a spear." As for His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, its literal meaning is understood by us, because in a single garden many rivers may flow, more than three or four. This is what it contains. Moreover, at the ends of the verses the singular is appropriate and the plural is not. It is also possible to say that the indefiniteness of ﴿and a river﴾ is for magnification. In Paradise there is a river that is the greatest and finest of rivers, and it is the one from al-Kawthar and from the Spring of Ridwan. Being near it is an honour and a cause for envy, and everyone has a seat beside it. The other rivers flow in Paradise and its people see them, but they do not see the one seated beside it. So He said ﴿in gardens and a river﴾, meaning that river beside which are the seats of the believers. In His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will test you with a river﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], the river is indefinite because it was not known to them. This also is a fine aspect. And on both of these aspects we need not say that *nahar* carries the meaning of the plural, since it is a generic noun.

We say: If we say that *fi nahar* means "among," then a person in this world can be among many springs surrounding him when he is on a raised place of the earth, and the springs gush out from it and flow, becoming rivers as they extend. But he cannot be among rivers; there are only two rivers at most. And if we say that what is meant is "beside a river," the same applies. And if we say it means a great sight with seats upon it, then we say: that river extends, reaching every one of them, and each has a seat beside it, with many springs following it. So the river is for honour, and the springs are for delight and recreation. Yet the great river also joins with many springs, so the river, with its oneness, takes the place of the springs with their multiplicity. All of this, considering the endings of the verses here and there, makes it fitting to mention the singular word here and the plural there.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 54, verse 55:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: How is ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ to be parsed? We say it may have two possible readings. The first is that it is in the form of a substitution (badal), as when someone says: "So-and-so is in such-and-such a town, in such-and-such a house." On this reading, "seat" (maq'ad) is one of the gardens, a place chosen for a distinction over the other places in the gardens. On this reading, the words ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign﴾ follow, because we have explained in one of the views that what is meant by ﴿in gardens and a river﴾ is "in gardens beside a river," and so He said: ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful.﴾ It may also be said that ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign﴾ is an attribute of "seat of truth." You say: "A dirham in the custody of a wealthy man is better than a dinar in the custody of a needy man, and a little in the custody of a trustworthy man is better than a lot in the custody of a treacherous man." So it is an attribute; otherwise it would not be good to make it a subject (mubtada'). The second is that ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ is like an attribute of "gardens and a river," meaning: in gardens and a river described as being in a seat of truth. You say: "A stop in the way of God is better than such-and-such," and ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign﴾ is an attribute after an attribute.

The second issue: His saying ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ indicates a staying that the word "majlis" (sitting place) does not indicate. This is because qa'ada (to sit/remain) and jalasa (to sit) are not, as is supposed, synonymous with no difference between them. Rather, there is a difference between them, but it is not apparent except to the discerning. The difference is that qu'ud is sitting in which there is actual and implied lingering. The following points show this:

The first: time is called maq'ad, but it is not called majlis, because of the length of staying in reality. From this comes the term qawa'id al-bayt (the foundations of the house). And elderly women are called qawa'id, but they are not called jawalis, because sitting does not indicate long lingering. So He mentioned qawa'id in both places, because it is something settled between permanence and stability in one state. A riding camel is called qa'ud because of the continuity of its sitting in an implied sense; even if not in reality, it is because it is preserved from loads and taken for riding, as if there were a kind of constant sitting in it, which implied this and was not intended for making someone sit.

The second: looking at the permutations of the letters. When you look at "q-‘-d" and permute it, you find the meaning of lingering in all of them. If you put the qaf first, you see qa'ada and qada'a with the same meaning, and from it taqada'a al-farash (the moths fell in a heap) meaning "rushed headlong." If you put the 'ayn first, you see 'aqada and 'adaqa with the meaning of lingering, very evident. In 'adaqa it is hidden; it is said: "a'diq bi-yadika al-dalw fi al-bi'r" (lower the bucket with your hand into the well) when he orders him to seek it after it has fallen into the well; and al-'awdaqah is a piece of wood with hooks on it, by which the bucket that has fallen into the well comes out. If you put the dal first, you see daqa'a and da'aqa, and lingering in daqa' is evident; al-daq'a is the dust clinging to the ground, and the poverty that is mudqa' is that which sticks its owner to the dust. Also in da'aqa, since al-da'q is a place trodden by animals with their hooves, so it becomes hard, its parts interlocked with one another, so that nothing in it moves from its place.

The third point: When the usages of qu'ud are considered, what we have mentioned becomes apparent. God the Exalted said: ﴿Those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than those with a disability, are not equal﴾ [al-Nisa: 95], and the meaning is one who has no one following him. He also said: ﴿positions for fighting﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121], while He said: ﴿Indeed, God loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾ [al-Saff: 4], thereby indicating great steadfastness. He said: ﴿When you meet a company, then stand firm﴾ [al-Anfal: 45]. So the maqa'id are the places where the fighter is in steadfastness and lingering. The use of maq'ada for the limb on which one sits also indicates this. When you know this difference between julus and qu'ud, benefits accrue to you, among them here: it indicates continuity of lingering and length of staying. Among them is His saying: ﴿on the right and on the left, a qa'id﴾ [Qaf: 17], for qa'id means companion and boon-companion. Then, when this is known, and it is said to the apparent exegetes: what is the benefit in choosing the word qa'id instead of the word jalis, although jalis is more well-known? Their answer would be that the end of the verses, from His saying ﴿the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and ﴿ready by me﴾ [Qaf: 23], and His saying ﴿every obstinate tyrant﴾ [Hud: 59], suits qa'id and not jalis; and the miraculous nature of the Qur'an is not in rhyme. When you consider what has been mentioned, a great spiritual and wise benefit becomes clear in placing the suitable word: because qa'id indicates that these two do not separate from him and continually sit with him. This is the miraculous aspect, because the poet chooses a corrupt word for the necessity of poetry and rhyme, and makes the meaning follow the word. God the Exalted has explained the wisdom as it should be, and brought the word in the best manner that is appropriate. Another benefit is in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when it is said to you, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; God will make room for you. And when it is said, "Rise up," then rise up﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11]. His saying ﴿make room﴾ indicates movement, and His saying ﴿rise up﴾ indicates leaving off sitting. He mentioned the assembly as an indication that this is a place of sitting, so it is not obligatory to remain in it, and it is not a maqad such that they should never leave it.

The third issue: ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ has two readings. The first: "maq'ad sidq" means "a righteous seat," as one says "a man of truth" for the righteous, and "a man of evil" for the corrupt; we have mentioned this in the surah ﴿Indeed, We have opened﴾ [al-Fath: 1], in His saying ﴿and you assumed an assumption of evil﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. The second: the truth meant is the opposite of falsehood. On this there are two views. The first: a seat of the truth of the one who reports it, who is God and His Messenger. The second: a seat attained by one who was truthful, who said that God is one and that Muhammad is His Messenger. It may also be said that what is meant is that it is a seat in which no falsehood is found, because God the Exalted is truthful and falsehood is impossible for Him, and whoever reaches Him is prevented from falsehood, because the cause of falsehood is ignorance, and the one who arrives at Him knows things as they are, and is self-sufficient by the bounty of God from lying to gain anything by his lie. So it is a seat of truth. The word "‘inda" (in the presence of) you know its meaning, and what is meant by it is nearness of rank and status, not nearness of space and place. His saying ﴿Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾: because nearness to kings is delightful; the more powerful the king, the more delighted is the one who draws near to him. In this there is an indication that the meaning of nearness to Him differs from the meaning of nearness to kings, for kings bring near those whom they love or whom they fear, lest they rebel against them and side with their enemy and overcome them. But God the Exalted said: ﴿All-Powerful﴾; He brings near no one except by His bounty.

And praise belongs to God, and His blessings be upon our master Muhammad, best of His creation, and upon his family and companions, and peace.
